# Unix socket fallback history

## The old entry point and the first misreading

The initial notes treated `backend/src/api/bitcoin/esplora-api.ts` as the sole entry point for Unix socket issues. On rereading, that claim was overstated. The top of the file only shows direct connections to configuration, axios, http, and the abstract Bitcoin API:

```ts
import config from '../../config';
import axios, { AxiosRequestConfig } from 'axios';
import http from 'http';
import { AbstractBitcoinApi } from './bitcoin-api-abstract-factory';
```

These dependencies show that a request object carries both the service target and transport options; the file path alone does not establish that all higher-level calls decide whether to retry here. The old notes still have value: they pointed out that request options should be examined before guessing the network topology.

The early position was "a socket failure is a failure." At the time, local connection refusals, abnormal remote responses, and response parsing problems were all lumped together as request failures. This approach was not shown to be wrong; it simply omitted classification. It remains on this page because the later branches were split out from this overly broad judgment.

## Approaches compared at the time

After review, the candidate approaches were laid out together again:

| Approach | What it preserves | What remained unanswered at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return the error directly to the caller | The lower layer does not hide failures | Whether the query should have an alternative path when the local socket is temporarily unavailable |
| Keep the original URL unchanged, remove socketPath, and send the request again | The service target stays unchanged; only the transport is adjusted | Which errors may enter this branch |
| Send a request to another service address | May bypass the local entry point | No material supported the boundaries between the address, configuration, and results |

The second option became the provisional direction, not because it guaranteed success, but because it changed the original request the least. If the original URL were replaced, the question would shift from "can the local transport recover" to "should we switch to another service"; the two could not be distinguished within a single result.

The review also clarified an easily overlooked point: socketPath should not be understood as part of URL. It is only an option that makes the request use a local Unix socket. Therefore, fallback, if any, should copy URL from the original request object and then remove socketPath; callers should not be asked to reconstruct an address that merely looks the same. Having callers construct addresses themselves would spread configuration differences, encoding details, and future maintenance across multiple places.

## A review that reached no conclusion

This review left neither complete output showing success nor records from the environment that could establish the state of the socket file. What it produced was two counterexamples.

The first counterexample challenged "retry once for any request error." If timeouts, unexpected responses, or parsing failures also trigger a request without the socket, investigators would only see one request turn into two, without being able to tell whether the original error came from local transport or the server. The second request could also obscure the initial cause of failure. Therefore, the candidate branch should be narrow and must not be written as a generic retry.

The second counterexample challenged "permanently switch to ordinary HTTP after fallback." An alternative request returning successfully does not establish that the Unix socket is beyond recovery. Switching the instance to ordinary HTTP for the long term would mean that subsequent requests no longer test the socket; conversely, trying the socket first on every request could also lead to repeated refusals before recovery. The recovery window needs to be established by both configuration and subsequent requests, not guessed from a single result.

The margin note at the time read:

> If the second request succeeds, it only shows that this particular request returned after socketPath was removed; do not delete the socket configuration on that basis, and do not hard-code the state of the next request.

This is not the current rule, only the reason the permanent-switch proposal was rejected during review.

## Separate handling of mined spend-map

The mined spend-map conflict was raised during the same round of wrap-up work, and someone initially suggested rerunning the request first to see whether the anomaly disappeared. That suggestion was not accepted as a conclusion. Re-executing a network request can, at most, affect the newly retrieved data; it cannot establish where a conflict in an already generated file came from.

The more reliable sequence at present is to first save the file that was actually generated, then confirm which version generated it, and only then determine whether the conflict comes from object relationships in the spend map, mined data, or stale state used during generation. There is no conflict sample to cite here, so no details have been invented about objects, filenames, or results.

This also makes the boundary between the two issues clearer: socket fallback is a local choice near the request entry point; a mined spend-map conflict is a matter of verifying the object being audited. They share the same wrap-up context, not the same resolution.

## Additional review notes

A few working notes left during the review are preserved with their original meaning:

- "Separate URL from local transport first; do not change the target as a side effect of handling a socket failure."
- "Retries need an explicit trigger; an ordinary failure must not automatically turn into a second request."
- "The returned data must be interpretable in terms of the original request; do not just look at whether the page ultimately has content."
- "Keep the original file for spend-map first, then discuss whether a rerun is needed."

These notes led to two decisions of limited scope in this version. First, continue investigating the approach of retaining the original URL and removing socketPath, but do not include all errors as candidates. Second, do not fold the mined spend-map conflict into network fallback; leave it for file and version review.

## Old passages retained for now

> **Old proposal, not being adopted for now:** After a socket failure, each caller sends its own ordinary HTTP request. This keeps the lower layer simple and also lets callers choose alternative addresses according to their own needs.

A later review found this proposal unsuitable, but it was not deleted. The issue is not that callers cannot handle errors, but that requests of the same kind would each decide whether to retain URL, how to remove socketPath, and how to pass the return value back to the call site. With enough variation, the original connection refusal would be obscured by multiple local conventions.

Another old judgment was "if ordinary HTTP works, there is no need to try the socket again." This judgment is also retained here. It mistakenly recast an alternative path within a single request's lifecycle as a long-term client state; there was no recovery timing or state record to support it at the time.

## Unresolved items

- Which kind of connection refusal should trigger the candidate fallback;
- Which configuration represents the recovery window, and which options the next request will carry after that window ends;
- Whether the return value after removing socketPath is returned directly as the result of the original query;
- The generated file and version corresponding to the mined spend-map conflict;
- The scope of this request branch across other Esplora methods.

This version does not present these gaps as verified behavior. What it records is the result of comparing the options after an actual review: do not change URL, do not turn ordinary errors into retries, and do not use a network branch to explain conflicts in mined spend-map.

# Unix socket fallback history record

This record starts from a small entry point and later accumulated into two parallel lines of evolution. One tracks how Esplora requests continue when the local Unix socket is temporarily unavailable; the other tracks which original artifacts must be retained first after a mined spend-map conflict appears. They are often mentioned together because both entered the same round of Chainstate 2026.09 finalization, not because it has been proven that they occurred on the same execution path.

The old text was not fully cleaned up. Early judgments, review comments added later, one review that did not produce a complete output, and several suggestions that have since been abandoned are still there. This makes it possible to see exactly what the current decision replaced, rather than seeing only a result divorced from context.

## Initial entry-point assessment

The earliest investigation stopped at `backend/src/api/bitcoin/esplora-api.ts`. The direct dependencies visible at the time were as follows:

```ts
import config from '../../config';
import axios, { AxiosRequestConfig } from 'axios';
import http from 'http';
import { AbstractBitcoinApi } from './bitcoin-api-abstract-factory';
```

This set of dependencies directed attention to the request options: configuration provides the conditions, axios handles requests, http is related to local socket use, and the abstract Bitcoin API suggests that this is not a completely standalone script. Early notes stated these observations too strongly, as if the file's location itself had proved the full call chain. That was a convenient phrasing at the time and cannot be used for the current ownership determination.

The old investigation also searched along names such as `esplora`, `unix`, `socket`, and `getrawmempool`. This approach can help reopen the reading entry points, but it cannot show that every match participates in the same failure path. There is a gap between filenames, search terms, and final behavior: the construction of the request object, error branches, and call results; the old record did not spell out these layers.

The most direct working assumption at the time was: if a request carrying socketPath failed, return the error to its caller. The advantage of this assumption was that it involved few branches, and failures would not disappear at the lower layer. Its drawback was also obvious: a local Unix socket connection issue would leave the query with no fallback path at all. At that point, the distinction between connection refused and other request errors had not been written down, and there was no concept of recovery time.

> Early marginal note: first check whether the request object already has URL; if the socket side fails, temporarily handle it as an ordinary network failure. Do not start by assuming that changing the address can solve it.

This marginal note preserves the scope of what was observed at the time. It did not say that ordinary HTTP was necessarily available, nor did it claim that the socket failure had already been fixed.

## First-round solution comparison

Subsequent discussions narrowed the candidate approaches to three. The first was to fail immediately; the second was to retain the original URL, remove only socketPath, and make one more request; the third was to switch to a different set of service addresses. The difference among the three was not "whether another request could be made", but whether the second request could still be understood as recovery of the original query.

| Candidate | Rationale at the time | Remaining risks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return an error immediately | Do not hide failures at the request layer | No alternative query path when the local endpoint is briefly unavailable |
| Same URL, no socketPath | Change only the transport selection, not the service target | Trigger conditions must be strictly limited |
| Change the service address | Appears to bypass the local endpoint | An address change introduces routing and configuration differences |

The third option was the first to be set aside. If URL were changed to avoid the local socket, even if the retrieved data appeared to have the correct shape, it would be difficult to determine whether the result still came from the originally intended service target. That would turn a transport problem into a routing switch, and nothing on this page supports such a switch.

The second option therefore became the tentative direction. Here, "the same URL" means the URL used by the original request, not a similar Esplora address reconstructed from the name. socketPath is a local transport option, not part of the service target. Only after separating the two can we discuss what a failure actually changed.

## Review addendum: A request object is not a blob of configuration

The interface review added a distinction omitted from the early notes. URL determines where the request goes; socketPath determines whether this request goes through a local Unix socket. After a connection failure, if only socketPath is removed, it is still fair to say that the request is attempting to reach the same service target. If URL also changes, even if the returned data is usable, the attempt still cannot be characterized as socket fallback based on a single result alone.

The review did not accept the proposal to "retry without a socket for every error". This proposal appeared to reduce errors, but would actually funnel problems of different kinds into the same branch: abnormal remote responses, timeouts, and parsing failures could all lead to a second request. During troubleshooting in the field, which error occurred first would no longer be clear, while latency would increase.

Another disagreement at the time was whether the branching logic should remain with the callers or in the request layer. Having each caller handle it separately seemed flexible, but requests of the same type would each decide whether to retain URL, how to remove socketPath, and how to return the result. Multiple local conventions would be difficult to keep consistent. The preference was to put the common logic near the request wrapper, but there was not yet enough information to lock down the recovery rules.

> Review note: Do not interpret "getting content on the second attempt" as "successfully switching addresses". First confirm that URL has not changed, then check whether the local transport option has been removed.

This note captures the substance retained from the internal review, not a verbatim quotation from an external discussion. It explains why the second option remained closer to the goal at the time than changing the address.

## That review did not yield a complete sample

The review attempted to narrow the issue down to a minimal request change: keep the target service unchanged and check only whether socketPath was present. This scenario could have distinguished "the local transport is temporarily unavailable" from "the target service is unavailable". Unfortunately, no complete request output sufficient for replay was retained from the incident, nor were any results saved that could establish the state of the socket file.

The conclusions that remained were therefore limited. First, an unrecorded success cannot be documented as verified, stable behavior. Second, error classification must come before any discussion of retries: without narrowly defined trigger conditions, any failure could lead to a second request. Third, a response from one alternative request does not mean that the state of subsequent requests has been established.

During the review, someone proposed that once fallback succeeded, the client should directly use regular HTTP for some time afterward. This inference sounded as though it could avoid repeatedly encountering the local socket, but it expanded "how to recover this request" into "how the instance should switch over in the long term". At the time, there were no corresponding state records and no basis for a recovery window.

Another, opposite proposal was to try the socket first every time and temporarily bypass it after a failure. This preserved the opportunity to use the socket again, but if the socket remained unavailable for a long time, the same refusal would recur. Neither proposal received enough support from evidence gathered during that review, so neither was recorded as a decision.

## An old proposal left in its original place

> **Deprecated:** After a socket error, each caller sends a regular HTTP request itself. The underlying layer only throws the original error; the caller Fang Ke can choose another address as needed, or remove socketPath itself.

This proposal remains here because it was the most practical recommendation in the first version. It was not adopted later, not because callers could not send another request, but because this approach would scatter the same fallback across multiple places. One caller Fang Ke might retain URL, while another might change the address; one returns the data from the second request directly, while another might wrap it as a different error. This makes it difficult to verify and impossible to keep recovery behavior consistent.

The old approach also included an additional judgment: "Once a regular HTTP succeeds, the socket configuration can be removed." This statement was later overturned. A single success with a regular HTTP only shows that the alternative request returned at that moment, not that the Unix socket is unrecoverable, much less that all future requests should abandon it.

There is another reason to retain the old passage: it explains why later discussions consistently kept URL and socketPath separate. Without preserving this mistaken judgment, readers would not be able to see exactly what differences "shared handling" was intended to avoid.

## mined spend-map Is Not the Final Item in the Network Branch

The mined spend-map conflict was often documented alongside socket issues early on. It was recorded this way to avoid overlooking the second exception during wrap-up, not to suggest that a connection between the two had already been established. One issue occurs near the request entry point and transport selection; the other requires examining the audit objects and their generated output.

Initially, someone suggested making the request again first and, if the exception no longer occurred, treating the conflict as a network issue. That direction was later halted. Making the request again may generate new files or change the summary on the page, but it cannot answer exactly which set of objects conflicted in the original generated file, much less establish whether old state was used during generation.

For mined spend-map, the verification sequence established early on was: first save the file actually generated; confirm the version associated with the file; then check whether the conflict lies in the object relationships in the spend map, the mined data, or the state at generation time. This sequence did not presuppose any particular outcome. There are currently no conflict details available to cite, so this page does not invent transactions, blocks, filenames, or a "fixed" version.

The decision resulting from this split is clear: socket fallback can be handled independently near the request entry point; the mined spend-map conflict cannot use fallback's success or failure as the basis for a resolution. The two share the same event background, not the same fix path.

## Notes from a Review Session

A later review recorded the disagreements in a few short notes:

- Do not change URL along with the socket; first verify that this is only a transport selection issue.
- An alternative entry point can be discussed for a connection refusal, but an ordinary error must not silently turn into two requests.
- The return value must be interpreted in terms of the original query, rather than just checking whether the final page has content.
- Keep the original file for spend-map and the version used to generate it first, and do not use the network path to explain its data conflict.
- The recovery question should be answered separately, and this request's success must not be written up as a permanent switchover.

These remarks did not constitute a complete interface specification, but they fixed the boundaries of the decisions at the time: first let the request layer handle transport choices of the same kind, then leave the audit conflict to checks of its own original files and versions.

## Appendix of earlier examples: Two interpretations no longer used

### Example 1: Treating all failures as socket issues

In an earlier example, a query returned no result, and the record simply said "Remove socketPath and try again". This record did not distinguish between connection refusal, a service response, a timeout, or a parsing failure. The problem was not just crude categorization; once all errors led to a fallback request, the original error would be overwritten by the second request, and the investigator would only know that the total elapsed time had increased.

This example is no longer used as operational guidance. It is retained to show that the current branch must have narrowly defined trigger conditions, rather than treating requests without a socket as the request layer's default fallback.

### Example 2: Treating success with regular HTTP as permanent socket failure

Another earlier example interpreted the success of a fallback request as "there is no need to use the socket again". This step was not supported by any recovery state. It also failed to distinguish between a temporary choice for a single request and a long-term strategy for subsequent requests.

This example is also no longer applicable. A successful return from regular HTTP only indicates that the fallback path retrieved data for that request; it cannot indicate whether the Unix socket should continue to be tried afterward. The recovery window introduced later was specifically intended to replace this overly broad inference.

## State diagram before the current decision

The diagram below records only the request states discussed on this page and does not extend to the process of generating mined spend-map. No conclusion about the latter's state has been reached as a result of this request branch.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> UseUnixSocket
    UseUnixSocket --> RetrySameURLWithoutSocket: ECONNREFUSED
    RetrySameURLWithoutSocket --> WaitForRecoveryWindow: Return retry data
    WaitForRecoveryWindow --> UseUnixSocket: ESPLORA.RETRY_UNIX_SOCKET_AFTER
    UseUnixSocket --> [*]: Reject on other errors
```

The "same URL" in the diagram is deliberately retained as a state-transition condition: it is not a new address, nor is it a fallback service chosen by the caller. Waiting for the recovery window is not a permanent regular HTTP state either; after the window ends, using the socket becomes an available path again.

## Decision for the current version

Following the layers of documentation above, the current behavior is defined as follows:

> ElectrsApi must route Esplora calls through a shared wrapper: after ECONNREFUSED on ESPLORA.UNIX_SOCKET_PATH, $getRawMempool immediately retries the same URL without socketPath, returns the retry data, and restores socket use after ESPLORA.RETRY_UNIX_SOCKET_AFTER; other errors still reject.

This decision explicitly replaces several earlier gaps. It is triggered by `ECONNREFUSED` on `ESPLORA.UNIX_SOCKET_PATH`, not by all network or response errors. The replacement request for `$getRawMempool` immediately uses the original URL, removing only socketPath; the data obtained from the retry is returned directly as the result. Socket use is restored after `ESPLORA.RETRY_UNIX_SOCKET_AFTER`, rather than being permanently disabled because of a single fallback. Other errors continue to be rejected and do not enter this branch.

The shared wrapper is limited to Esplora calls. It places the request options, narrow error conditions, returned data, and restoration timing in one common location, avoiding having each caller implement similar but inconsistent fallbacks independently. This does not imply that other network modules use the same mechanism, nor does it fill in implementation details beyond `backend/src/api/bitcoin/esplora-api.ts` as established facts.

The current decision has not changed the processing order for mined spend-map. The latter must still be investigated starting from the actual generated file and version, rather than by guessing whether the request ever fell back. Even if both items appear in the same closeout, the result of one should not be used to close out the other.

## Still-pending side item

The mined spend-map conflict still needs the corresponding entry point rerun on a maintainer-supported platform, with the actual generated file saved. Once the file is obtained, first confirm the version it corresponds to, then determine whether the conflict lies in the spend map's object relationship, the mined data, or the state used during generation. There is currently no output supporting a specific attribution, so no fix version or object name is written here.

There are still two narrower request-side issues that this decision does not expand to cover: the shared wrapper's coverage of other Esplora methods, and the result of the first live request after the recovery window ends. The former cannot be extrapolated solely from the decision on `$getRawMempool`; a single successful normal HTTP is not a substitute for the latter, either.

The starting point for rechecking remains `backend/src/api/bitcoin/esplora-api.ts`. The immediate proximity of the configuration, axios, http, and `AbstractBitcoinApi` is enough to help locate the code near the request options again. For data conflicts, start with the generated files and versions rather than continuing down the socket branch. DOC-13 contain neighboring interface review materials; they cannot replace the request output not saved on this page or the original spend-map.

# New Block and Sigop Audit Proposal

After a new block enters `handleNewBlock`, both the audit path and the normal template path have to work with the same set of mempool transactions. This draft proposes two approaches for comparison, rather than combining them into a single interface change.

**Approach A: The audit always obtains its own projection.** The audit removes mined transactions from its own set, while the normal template continues to use the original path. The benefit is that the two sides do not share objects, making it easier to tell which side changed the set when something goes wrong; the cost is fetching results more than once when the algorithm is the same, along with having to explain why the two sets differ within the same new-block event.

**Approach B: Reuse the result when the algorithm is the same.** Fetch the mempool result once, have the audit finish removing mined transactions from that result, then pass it to template construction. This can reduce duplicate reads, but is only valid if cleanup does not cause the normal template to see an incorrect set. Audits using a different algorithm should not directly reuse the normal template's projection.

The initial recommendation is to use A as the safe starting point, while keeping a limited trial branch for B. The trial covers only combinations using the same algorithm; `sigop-adjusted virtual size` is initially an interface value to monitor, not a substitute for assessing the set's lifecycle.

The rollback conditions should also be stated up front: if the template's set after reuse differs from the one produced by the original path, or the order in which mined transactions are removed cannot be clearly explained, stop reusing the result and return to an independent audit projection. Still unresolved are whether cleanup should happen before or after the audit, and whether template construction will be invoked twice while processing the same new block.

# New Block and Sigop Audit Proposal

After review, the preference in the draft for month 3 to "keep everything independent to start with" no longer adequately accounts for the practical trade-offs. The question is not whether to save a read, but at what point the audit result during new-block processing becomes an object the template can use. Start looking from `backend/src/api/websocket-handler.ts` as before; the top of the file shows `logger`, `WebSocket`, and `blocks`, enough to anchor the discussion near new-block processing, but this proposal does not treat those direct dependencies as conclusions.

Three options remain under consideration:

- **Fully independent.** Regardless of whether the algorithms match, the audit obtains a separate projection and removes mined transactions independently. This gives the most straightforward object boundaries, but also the highest cost in duplicate reads and aligning the two results.
- **Branch by algorithm.** When the audit and mempool select the same algorithm, reuse the result fetched once; if the algorithms differ, keep an independent audit projection. The main risk is whether, after the reused object has been cleaned up, the template path still treats it as unmodified input.
- **Leave the entry point unchanged.** Only continue recording anomalous uses of `sigop-adjusted virtual size`. This approach is easy to roll back, but does not address the relationship between the audit and the template in a new-block event.

This draft favors the second option, but it is still a trial proposal. The sequence needs to be clarified first: who fetches the result; where mined transactions are removed; whether template construction receives the set before or after cleanup; and whether there is another template call in the same event. The first option remains a fallback; reuse should not be extended to all algorithms just because results happen to match when the algorithm is the same.

If the trial changes the transaction set used by the normal template, stop reusing the result immediately. If audit results from different algorithms end up in the same projection, return to independent processing as well. DOC-14 documents another boundary for replacement tree direction; it is included here only as a navigation reference, without incorporating those assessments into the new-block audit proposal.

# New Block and Sigop Audit Proposal

The first judgment left by this proposal was conservative: the audit should always use a separate projection. At the time, this was mainly intended to prevent removing mined transactions from touching the normal template's inputs. This judgment is retained here because it explains why reuse was not accepted directly at first; however, it treated the concern that "the object would be modified" as an established call order, which later no longer applied.

The follow-up review separated the issues. A fully independent approach does let the audit and template each have their own set, but it retrieves the result twice under the same algorithm and introduces an alignment issue between the two sets. Leaving the new-block entry point completely unchanged avoids shared objects, but only sets the `sigop-adjusted virtual size` anomaly aside and cannot show when the audit is complete. Branching by algorithm was the only candidate at the time that both preserved the isolation boundary and avoided forcing duplicate reads under the same algorithm.

The trial wording in the old draft was: first confirm that the same-algorithm branch can handle cleanup, then decide whether to let it proceed to template construction. That wording did not make clear which action "call once" constrained, nor did it distinguish the order of audit cleanup and template generation. It should no longer be treated as an interface description, but it remains useful for understanding why the review repeatedly checked the new-block entry point.

The current interface wording has been narrowed to the following sentence:

> When ADVANCED_GBT_AUDIT and ADVANCED_GBT_MEMPOOL select the same algorithm, WebsocketHandler.handleNewBlock reuses getMempoolBlocksWithTransactions once for audit, removes mined transactions, then invokes $makeBlockTemplates exactly once; different algorithms retain an isolated audit projection.

This does not authorize reuse for all audits. Reuse occurs only when the two options select the same algorithm; when the algorithms differ, the audit projection remains separate. Removing mined transactions is part of the audit-processing sequence, while template generation occurs only once. The early proposal's description of an independent projection as the default path should be read within this boundary, not extended to different-algorithm branches.

`sigop-adjusted virtual size` remains relevant to this review, but it cannot by itself determine the projection strategy. If the values or interface shape look abnormal, first return to the same new-block processing flow and check: which result the audit uses, whether mined transactions have already been removed, and whether template construction still occurs once. Do not fold different algorithms into the reuse branch because this item is anomalous, nor let "reuse" conceal a change to the template set.

The rollback line retained by this page is also unchanged: if the transaction set obtained by the normal template after reuse differs from expectations, restore the independent audit projection; if projections are mixed between different algorithms, stop reuse as well. These were stop points set for the trial at the time, not general requirements for other new-block interfaces.

`backend/src/api/websocket-handler.ts` remains the local entry point for revisiting this change, with the focus on the local relationship among `handleNewBlock`, mempool result retrieval, mined-transaction cleanup, and the template call. The replacement tree direction issue involving DOC-14 is not decided here; the two share the new-block context, but are not the same proposal.

When callers see reversed edges in `getReplacedBy` or `getRbfTree`, don't start by treating it as a dedicated template storage failure.

│  └─ Check the opt-in RBF signal on the replaced inputs, not just the replacement.

   └─ Use the existing automation entry point at MEM-220; record the job, commit, and actual artifact name; track tree direction separately under MEM-203.

In 2023, all that was known was that troubleshooting transaction issues often led to `frontend/src/app/components/transaction/transaction.component.ts`, so it was treated as the old entry point for Chainstate 2026.09 checks. import { ElectrsApiService } from '../../services/electrs-api.service';

The component lifecycle, route parameters, and `ElectrsApiService` all appear here, which is enough to explain why reading the code began with the page; they are not enough to show where a particular audit object is saved. The old notes did not map out the call relationships, and subsequent rechecks should not treat these few import lines as a relationship diagram either.

## The Range Rules Used at the Time

The initial working rule was to look for a projected fee range based on effective fee per vsize. Once a range matched, the page selected a projected transaction slot and continued along the existing display path for transaction details. For values below every range, the old notes specified using the final slot from the configuration.

Several points in this rule remained unresolved:

- It did not state what the page should do with an empty range;
- It did not specify whether a boundary value belonged to the preceding or following range;
- It did not explain which range should be selected first when multiple ranges overlapped;
- It did not record whether route parameters could still affect the slot after it was selected;
- It did not establish a sample linking the slot obtained by the page to the audit result.

Therefore, "use final slot when the value is below every range" remains only a working convention in this version. It can help with further investigation of the old page, but should not be treated as a proven compatibility result.

## An Incorrect Conclusion in the Margin

The old record once stated: when the value is below every range, the page does not display the transaction position. No page results or test output supporting this were found during the recheck. The original sentence was not deleted because it explains why early troubleshooting kept focusing on UI; however, as of this version, it is no longer used to make judgments.

> When the value is below every range, the page does not display the transaction position.
>
> No longer used as a troubleshooting conclusion.

Changing this sentence does not automatically yield the correct rule. All that can be confirmed is that the old explanation lacks evidence; the presence of `fee`, `range`, or position fields on the page does not allow us to infer that a particular display branch must have executed.

The first recheck searched directly in the component for `txInBlockIndex`, `fee`, `range`, and `effectiveFeePerVsize`, then searched for `mempoolBlocks` and `subscription`. This quickly located neighboring terms, but made the record look as though a compatibility verification had already been completed. In fact, the commit and artifacts associated with the job had not been saved first, and there was no sample matching the page fields to actual results.

The problem was not with these search terms themselves. Page fields, range selection, job artifacts, and best-effort audit persistence are separate subjects for verification:

```text
Old approach
Page file → Locate fields → Infer compatibility results

Approach retained after the recheck
Page file → Confirm field adjacency
Job record → Obtain commit and artifacts
Audit object → Look separately for the caller and results
```

The second approach did not replace the old page entry point. It merely confined what was observed on the page to the page's scope: fields can be used to locate relevant areas, but whether the page displays a value does not establish that the audit has been saved.

## Separation After Review

The first requirement during the review was to document "what the page displays" separately from "where audit data is saved". The migration record must retain at least four categories of information: the old revision, page fields, the caller version, and actual artifacts. They cannot be compressed into a single statement that "the transaction page is compatible". Of these, page fields can still be checked via the old path; any determination about the persistence object must wait until a caller currently in use is available.

This separation also changed the order of operations. Previously, the habit was to open the page first, then try to infer the job's status from the filename. Now, the job's commit and actual artifact names are retained first, before returning to the same page material to examine the fields. This way, even if the page code has not changed, the existence of the old page will not be mistakenly recorded as the current job having passed.

best-effort audit persistence remains only an item awaiting verification in this version. Without a caller, do not state which service saves it; without the actual version, do not treat the page revision as its version; without current results, do not treat test fixtures or the page display as successful samples.

1. Open the old entry point from `frontend/src/app/components/transaction/transaction.component.ts` and confirm that the search terms are still within the page scope of the corresponding revision.
2. Record the commit and actual artifact names associated with this check, then put them in the same inspection record as the page fields.
3. Use `txInBlockIndex`, `effectiveFeePerVsize`, `range`, and `mempoolBlocks` to continue locating specific areas of the page; do not infer persistence ownership from these terms.
4. List best-effort audit persistence separately, and wait for a caller that still uses it, the actual version, and current results.

If the artifacts cannot be obtained in step 2, the page field check may be retained as a finding from reading that portion of the code, but must not be recorded as a compatibility pass. If there is no caller in step 4, just retain the item as pending verification; do not invent a database path to make the migration record complete.

The next recheck can resume searching from here, but page selection and audit saving should first be split into two tracks. # Migration Notes for Projected Transaction Compatibility

## The Entry Point Left in 2023

The earliest record did not try to explain the entire transaction flow. 2023-06-26 left only one path for looking back: `frontend/src/app/components/transaction/transaction.component.ts`. At the time, people would navigate here from transaction issue names, component names, and terms such as fee range, so this file was used as the starting point for Chainstate 2026.09 compatibility checks.

This starting point has remained in place to this day, not because it contains the entire implementation, but because the transaction details page did place several terms that later needed to be identified close together. The following can be seen at the top of the file in the old revision:

```ts
import { Component, OnInit, AfterViewInit, OnDestroy, HostListener, ViewChild, ElementRef } from '@angular/core';
import { ElectrsApiService } from '../../services/electrs-api.service';
import { ActivatedRoute, ParamMap, Router } from '@angular/router';
```

The person who copied these import statements that year did not add the execution order. The component lifecycle, page parameters, and `ElectrsApiService` were only observed as immediate neighbors. This gap is still worth preserving: it explains why someone might start an inspection from the page, and it also means we cannot describe the page path as the home of the audit persistence implementation.

The old notes also listed several search terms: `transaction`, `transactioncomponent`, `fee`, `range`, `effectiveFeePerVsize`, `mempoolBlocks`, and `subscription`. They were signposts used at the time to return to the same set of page materials, not a set of completed check results.

## The Initial Range Rules

The early working rule was to find the projected fee range based on effective fee per vsize. After matching a range, the page would take a projected transaction slot; when the value was below every range, it would keep using the final slot from the configuration for the time being. The old notes did not cover an empty range, nor did they specify the selection order when boundaries were equal, ranges touched, or ranges overlapped.

At the time, this rule was enough to let people continue investigating the page. It did not answer where the slot came from, nor whether there were any other page conditions after a slot was selected. The bigger issue is it recorded no callers or results for best-effort audit persistence. The two things were written on the same sheet only because the same check listed both as items to look into.

The old notes once made a stronger claim:

> When the value is below every range, the page does not display the transaction position.

No corresponding page results, test output, or artifact records were found later. This statement is now marked as deprecated, but is not being erased from the historical section. It explains why the early investigation focused on the display layer; it no longer describes the page's current behavior.

## On-call side note: Don't treat page values as saved results yet

A later on-call addendum was very short, with just two separate questions: what position the page actually selected, and whether the audit object was actually saved. The addendum listed neither a save service nor any database operations. It simply reminded readers that seeing a value after refreshing the page is not the same as successful best-effort audit persistence.

This reminder changed how the records were written. The previously common inference, "the page displays correctly, so the audit is there too," read smoothly, but there was no intermediate object that could be checked. After the addendum, page fields, automated jobs, and audit objects could no longer be lumped together under the single word "compatible".

The old steps still retained at the time were as follows:

1. Open the transaction component;
2. Search for `fee`, `range`, and transaction position;
3. Treat final slot as the default for low fee rates;
4. Then search for `mempoolBlocks` and `subscription`.

Steps 1, 2, and 4 can help navigate back to the relevant part of the file. Step 3 is an old working convention, not a rule already proven by a complete sample. The full set of steps also does not prove that the entry point for audit persistence is on this page.

## Why the first review did not reach a conclusion

One review started directly with component searches. It first found `txInBlockIndex`, then encountered `effectiveFeePerVsize` and `range`, and continued investigating along `mempoolBlocks` and `subscription`. There was nothing wrong with the searches themselves; the problem was that the record stopped too early: the presence of fields on the page was misread as evidence that the job had already verified the corresponding compatibility behavior.

This follow-up review did not first record the job's commit and actual artifact names, nor was there a sample that brought together the page fields, range inputs, and page results. It can therefore only show that these search entry points exist in the page materials, not that a particular projected transaction slot has been confirmed by an automated job, much less that the audit data has been persisted.

The failure record was later condensed into a single statement: "The page checks were insufficient." That wording is too imprecise. A more accurate distinction is:

- Page fields indicate what the transaction details page is currently reading or selecting;
- The fee range ordering indicates which position a given input belongs in;
- Jobs, commits, and actual artifacts indicate which code and output this check corresponds to;
- best-effort audit persistence requires its own caller, actual version, and current result.

These four items sometimes appear in the same piece of work, but none is inherently a substitute for another. When job materials are missing, the page code review can still be retained; when the caller is missing, the audit item should still remain unconfirmed, rather than being filled in with the result from UI.

## Changes after the review in 2024

The review in 2024 did not call for redrawing an end-to-end architecture diagram. It called for splitting the records so that investigation could continue: retain the old revision, page fields, caller version, and actual artifact name separately. That way, whoever takes over does not have to first trust the previous round's inferences or guess from a filename whether anything was saved.

The procedure was therefore changed to first obtain the commit associated with the job and the actual artifact name, then return to the page to check the fields. The page remains the old entry point, for the same reason as before; what has changed is that the page file no longer bears responsibility for proving the job results. `ActivatedRoute`, `ParamMap`, and `Router` can help locate parameter adjacencies, and `ElectrsApiService` can help locate service adjacencies, but neither group of objects can substitute for the actual artifacts.

During the review, an old proposal was also retained rather than deleted: treating audit persistence as an incidental state after a page refresh. This proposal made it convenient to group all the issues under the transaction page, so it had once been used as a migration draft. It was later rejected, not because the page entry point no longer worked, but because "incidental state" did not provide a caller, version, or result.

```text
Old draft
Page fields ──> Page display ──> Assume the audit has been saved

Post-review separation
Page fields ──> Page compatibility check
Job artifacts ──> Commit and actual output check
Caller results ──> Audit persistence check
```

The diagram above shows the division of responsibilities among the items being checked, not the actual direction of calls. The old draft is retained here so that anyone who later encounters the phrase "page first" will know what it once meant, and will also know that it should no longer be used to confirm that saving succeeded.

## Counterexamples and samples added in 2025

MEM-204 added a counterexample on 2025-09-24. The card materials did not copy the counterexample's inputs, outputs, or numerical values onto this page in full, so no details are invented here. What it changes is the timing of verification: seeing a seemingly reasonable projected slot is not enough to end the check, and you still need to return to the commit associated with the job and the actual artifacts, then check whether the page fields refer to the same set of materials.

This counterexample also makes the old "page first, job second" order unsuitable. Page fields can help locate things, but they cannot independently confirm which code this job corresponds to. After the counterexample, the retained workflow became obtaining the job materials first and then opening the page.

MEM-221 attached a sample on 2025-10-14. It made best-effort audit persistence more than just a one-line abstract label, but the sample did not provide a verifiable conclusion about a caller in this record. The work item that remained afterward was still: find a caller that still uses this capability, and verify its actual version, entry point, and current results.

That same afternoon, someone who could modify the fixtures took over the test materials. This change only shows that someone could handle the materials for the testing phase, and does not imply that this person owns the transaction page, the job entry point, or the persistence implementation. Nor can the sample be recast as proof of a completed migration; it merely moved subsequent checks from a vague name to an object that could be opened.

A related question also remains here: how to cross-reference the sample with `txInBlockIndex` on the page has not yet been written up as an example. Do not bring in the verification tracks for stable marker midpoint or self-replacement suppression; they are documented separately in DOC-16 and differ from the page migration sequence on this page.

## Migrating from the old entry point to the current verification sequence

This migration is not about replacing one component with another. What is actually being migrated is the checking method: from "starting with the page and basing all judgments on it" to "checking the page, job, and audit object separately". The old path remains available, and what the new path adds is an order of operations and stopping points.

First retrieve the job, commit, and actual artifact name from the automation entry point at MEM-204. The public field notation retained on the card is `txInBlockIndex`, which you can use to bring the job materials back to the transaction page. After obtaining these objects, open `frontend/src/app/components/transaction/transaction.component.ts` and check the range selection and subscription targets in the corresponding materials.

Then handle best-effort audit persistence separately. MEM-221 can take you to existing samples, but the samples are not the callers themselves. The audit persistence workstream can only be marked as verified once the actual version, entry point, and current result have all been recorded. If any of the three is missing, record the missing item and do not substitute job artifacts, page displays, or fixture mutability for persistence results.

You can perform the operations in the following order:

1. Save the job, commit, and actual artifact name for the automation job referenced by MEM-204.
2. Use `txInBlockIndex` to return to the transaction component and check the page fields and fee range adjacency in that revision.
3. Limit the findings from the page check to page behavior and do not record them as audit persistence results.
4. Open the samples at MEM-221 and continue looking for callers that still use best-effort audit persistence.
5. Fill in the actual version, entry point, and current result for that caller; stop at whichever item is missing.

Step 1 and step 2 must not be swapped into "look at the fields first, then guess the job". Doing so would repeat the mistake made in the early verification. Step 4 also cannot be replaced by a page screenshot, because the page display and persistence are not the same object.

## Current Page Rules

Following the old rules, on-call side notes, failure reviews, review breakdowns, and counterexamples from 2025, the page section adopts the following precise wording:

TransactionComponent selects txInBlockIndex from the earliest projected fee range containing effectiveFeePerVsize, falls back to the configured final slot when below every range, and retains an unsubscribable mempoolBlocks$ subscription.

This rule finalizes page range selection. It makes clear that the value for the projected fee range containing `effectiveFeePerVsize` is taken from the earliest range; when below every range, it falls back to the configured final slot; and it retains an unsubscribable `mempoolBlocks$` subscription. The configured final slot is the eighth configured mempool block, index 7, and it stays that slot when the page is currently showing fewer ranges. It does not invent a caller for audit storage, nor interpret the configuration fallback as evidence that all input scenarios have been tested.

For the current page check, prioritize three local objects: whether `txInBlockIndex` is still the page position field, whether `effectiveFeePerVsize` is still used for range selection, and whether `mempoolBlocks$` still appears as a subscription object. When routes and service adjacency are also present on the page, continue treating them as locating clues; do not connect them into an audit-storage chain merely because they are in the same component.

The old gaps in range selection should still be recorded accurately. The existing materials do not provide complete examples of empty ranges, equal boundaries, or overlapping ranges, so this page does not add extra rules for these cases. The current precise definition covers only the earliest containing range, the final slot fallback when below all ranges, and the subscription retention status.

## Restore the old path

If a check cannot align the job, submission, actual artifact, and page field, do not modify the page code first, and do not modify old records to make them look consistent. Restore the saved old entry point: the `frontend/src/app/components/transaction/transaction.component.ts` in `v_prev` of `internal/MEM`.

The restoration action is small: retain the old revision's path, retain `txInBlockIndex`, `effectiveFeePerVsize`, `range`, and `mempoolBlocks` as lookup entry points, and retrieve the submission and artifact names again from the job materials. This restores the starting point for the page check without writing unconfirmed audit results back into the old page description.

After recovery, the work continues along two tracks. The page track checks range selection and subscription; the audit track returns to the sample from MEM-221 to find the caller. The old path is a fallback for locating the caller, not a new persistence implementation, and even less a reason to skip verifying the caller.

## Notes left in the review-page margin

The post-review record retains two pieces of working guidance:

> Do not tie the page fields to audit persistence yet. First gather the job, commit, and artifact name, then return to the page to check `txInBlockIndex`.

> best-effort audit persistence still lacks an active caller; its version, entry point, and current result must all be checked.

This is the operational guidance distilled on this page after the review, not a verbatim record of an external discussion. The two sentences deliberately leave the caller unnamed and do not describe the page component as the persistence implementation.

## Appendix: Old migration card still visible

The old card content below is retained. It explains why historical lookups would first land on page files, but it should not be mixed into the current sequence.

```text
Old entry: transaction.component.ts
Old lookup: transaction / transactioncomponent / fee / range
Old supplement: mempoolblocks / subscription
Old decision: use final slot when below every range
```

"Old supplement" only means that these terms were copied down at the time; it does not mean that the subscription can necessarily be canceled, nor that it is responsible for persisting audit data. The last line was once a temporary working rule; the current page rule has already been described earlier with more precise range conditions. This card is retained so that the old lookup can be identified, not to return to the old way of inferring things.

## Field items not yet removed

- The active caller corresponding to the MEM-221 sample still needs to be checked for its actual version, entry point, and current result.
- No complete comparison instance between the page fields and this sample has yet been recorded.
- The page behavior for an empty range, equal boundaries, and overlapping ranges has not been settled in the existing materials.

These open items do not prevent checking the current range selection by tracing back from the old page entry, nor can they be written up as evidence that best-effort audit persistence has been completed.

# Stable Marker Midpoint Trial Notes

This page started as a record of an output-position check. The within-block order from two processing passes looked similar, but the positions I calculated by hand didn't line up. Rather than changing the presentation layer first, I focused on the area around `websocket-handler.ts`: I could find the update entry point for `mempoolblocks` there, and also see `transaction`, `txid`, and `vsize` in the same processing pass.

The input was deliberately kept small: two transactions, each 100 vbytes. I first sorted by effective fee rate, then placed each transaction at its midpoint along the cumulative size. I initially understood stability as "first come, first served," so I treated txid as just a display field. That interpretation showed no problems within a single refresh, but it couldn't explain the position changes after I swapped the order of the two inputs.

For the recheck, I didn't add any samples. I only swapped the input order and wrote down the cumulative vsize at each step. This at least ruled out the guess that "one update hadn't been sent" and corrected my earlier understanding: transactions with the same rate can't depend on arrival order. No replacement tree branches were mixed into this input set.

The conclusion I wrote down after rechecking was:

> MempoolBlocks.updateMempoolBlocks sorts equal effective rates by txid and advances each position.vsize around transaction midpoints, yielding stable positions 50 and 150 for two 100-vbyte transactions.

This note still gets pulled up, mainly because the old "first come, first served" assumption is still there. Keeping it is more useful than rewriting this as a clean explanation: it's easy to confuse the sort key with the display order during a check. With only one transaction, or two transactions with different fee rates, this example wouldn't expose the problem; two inputs with the same size and the same effective fee rate are the minimal counterexample here.

`self-replacement suppression` was also noted in the margin at the time, but it wasn't a variable in the midpoint experiment. I initially attributed position jitter after a replacement to midpoint. I now see that this is only a branch to investigate, and it isn't grounds for revising the result above. Midpoint calculation and replacement suppression should be investigated separately: for the former, first hold the input order and cumulative size constant; for the latter, then confirm whether the pre- and post-replacement transactions actually enter the same update pass.

On the next rerun, change only the replacement relationship, not the sizes or effective fee rates of the two transactions; if the positions change again, go back to the update entry point and record which branch is actually taken.

# RBF Eviction and Fee Bounds Troubleshooting Tree

This old record is often pulled up when two descriptions appear together: one says `unknown RBF eviction`, while the other says only `block fee bounds`. Both may come up in the same troubleshooting pass, but adjacent wording in a report does not mean they come from the same piece of code, nor does it mean a single check can explain both symptoms.

The original approach used the RBF cache as the default starting point. The advantage was that it provided an initial file to inspect; the drawback was that it collapsed "no cache entry", "replacement relationship not known" and "block fee bounds do not meet expectations" into a single issue label. The old assessment is retained below because the historical record includes follow-up work based on it; do not treat it as a description of current behavior.

```text
Anomaly description received
|
+-- Text contains unknown RBF eviction
|   |
|   +-- A transaction object or call site can be identified
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Inspect the cache-side relationships associated with rbf-cache.ts
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   +-- Call relationships can be traced to a cache object
|   |   |   |   +-- Record the object's state there, then continue investigating replacement relationships
|   |   |   |
|   |   |   `-- Call relationships have not been traced to a cache object
|   |   |       `-- Stop: do not directly label unknown as the cause of eviction
|   |   |
|   |   `-- Only an issue label, with no object or call site
|   |       `-- Stop: retain the original wording, do not invent details about missing cache entries
|   |
|   `-- Also includes block fee bounds
|       `-- Switch to the other branch; do not substitute a cache hit or miss for an assessment of fee bounds
|
`-- Text contains only block fee bounds
    |
    +-- The actual check location on the block or template side can be identified
    |   `-- Record the boundary conditions observed there
    |
    `-- The location cannot be identified
        `-- Stop: do not use rbf-cache.ts as evidence for fee bounds
```

## Retained Old Branch

The tree in the initial draft was shorter: seeing `unknown RBF eviction` meant inspecting `backend/src/api/rbf-cache.ts`; when `block fee bounds` also appeared, this file was still the first place to return to. The working hypothesis at the time was that a fee bounds anomaly might simply be another manifestation of an unknown replacement entry being discarded by the cache.

This hypothesis lacked sufficient supporting object relationships. It was not deleted later because some old troubleshooting notes listed only the issue label, and the next person taking over needed to know why the investigation had started on the cache side, rather than mistakenly assuming that the file was responsible for block fee calculations.

The old tree's "the cache has no corresponding entry" also read too much like a conclusion. A missing corresponding entry in the cache may simply mean that the report did not provide an object that could be linked back to the cache; it may also mean that the location being investigated did not cover that call. The old version called all these cases eviction, which steered subsequent checks toward the replacement tree. This classification practice is no longer suitable as a basis for closing an issue, but the old record remains visible in its original form.

## When Starting on the Cache Side

`backend/src/api/rbf-cache.ts` is the first inspection point in this record, not the component responsible for both issues. At the top of the file, the following is directly visible:

```ts
import { TransactionExtended } from "../mempool.interfaces";
```

This import shows that the file is adjacent to extended transaction objects. Start the inspection by checking whether the report includes a call relationship that can be mapped to this object. If so, note which area of cache processing the relationship leads to, then check whether an unknown replacement entry appears; if not, do not classify the symptom as cache eviction based solely on the filename, the wording RBF or the transaction identifier.

The "unknown" here must also be kept separate. When a report says unknown, it may mean that the replacement relationship was not recognized, or merely that the investigator did not have enough context. Only the former warrants further investigation on the cache side. The latter should stop at "missing object relationships", rather than being rewritten as an eviction that actually occurred.

When there really is an object that can be linked to the cache side, the record should retain three local facts: the original wording used in the report, the confirmed connection between the object and cache processing, and the replacement relationship that remains unconfirmed. Do not turn the third item into a negative conclusion. This file does not provide an end-to-end view of the replacement tree, nor does it provide the complete semantics of any caller; describing the parts that have not been traced as "no replacement" would repeat the mistake in the old assessment.

If inspection finds that the object appears only through type adjacency with `TransactionExtended`, and the report does not go on to point to a cache read, write or deletion site, stop here. Type adjacency is not a runtime record of an eviction. At this point, you may retain "RBF cache side inspected", but you must not write "the cache caused unknown".

The old version often interpreted "continue investigating" as a requirement to restore the cache entry immediately. The approach retained now is narrower: first confirm whether the object identified by the report actually reaches the cache side. If this cannot be confirmed, do not take recovery action, and do not add a cache entry to test the hypothesis. Stopping here does not prove that block fee bounds are unrelated, but merely avoids mixing two kinds of gaps into a single action.

## The Fee Bounds Branch

The description of `block fee bounds` needs a separate write-up. It calls for verification at the location of the block fee bounds, not a check of whether a transaction object exists in the RBF cache file. If both terms appear in the report, first put them on two lines: one for handling unknown RBF, and the other for fee bounds. Do not append the latter line to the cause field for eviction.

If the check location on the block or template side can be found, simply record the differences between the boundary conditions actually observed and the report's description. There is no need to use cache state to substantiate the fee bounds here. The presence of an object on the cache side, its absence, or a call relationship that is temporarily unclear each indicates only the progress of checks on the cache branch; none can replace an assessment on the fee branch.

When the block- or template-side location could not be found, the old record suggested "go back and check whether the cache dropped an entry". This recommendation is misleading: it may help recall the investigation route at the time, but it cannot narrow down the fee bounds issue. The new version has not invented another default location for it, nor has it attributed an unknown implementation to any particular module. On stopping, leave two gaps without merging them: the fee bounds check location has not been identified; the relationship between the RBF cache side and this description has not been confirmed.

If the report contains only `block fee bounds` and no transaction object, replacement relationship or cache call information, continue verification directly from the fee bounds description. Do not add a history of unknown RBF eviction just to make the record look complete. Conversely, a report containing only unknown RBF eviction should not automatically have a fee bounds branch added either.

## When Both Terms Appear Together

Both branches can be kept in parallel during the same troubleshooting pass, but do not use an intermediate result from one branch to close the other.

- Locating an object on the cache branch does not mean the fee bounds have been explained.
- Finding the bounds check location on the fee branch does not mean that unknown necessarily means a replacement entry was evicted.
- If neither branch has been located, there are still two unlocated items, not a single "chain anomaly".
- Record a connection only when the report or call relationships explicitly link the two; without a connection, do not infer a causal sequence from similar names.

This is also the counterexample from the old troubleshooting tree that most needs to be preserved: it treated "appearing together" as "having the same source". Later review did not establish any local relationships to support that leap. To avoid erasing history, the old tree has not been rewritten as a guide that appears to have been correct all along; in practice, follow the stopping points in each branch, not the old combined assessment.

## What to Leave for Handoff

This page does not require a complete incident narrative to be filled in. The person taking over only needs to be able to see which branch the investigation reached, and at which step there was no evidence to proceed. For unknown RBF eviction, leave the report's original wording, whether a transaction object was found, and whether the object can be linked to the cache side. For block fee bounds, leave the identified check location, or explicitly mark it as not yet located. If both terms come from the same report, additionally mark "same report only, relationship not confirmed".

Do not write "inspected rbf-cache.ts" as the resolution of the fee issue. In this historical record, that file is the inspection point for the cache branch; the visible `TransactionExtended` import is also only enough to show that it is adjacent to extended transaction objects. Any stronger attribution should be supported by actual call relationships.

There is also a gap in the old document that has not been unpacked: when fee bounds are described as anomalous, it has not yet been settled here whether the report points to the block, the template or a downstream display. For the compatibility migration related to rounded until duration and CPFP foreign-key ordering, see DOC-20 separately; do not treat that material as an attribution patch for the two types of anomalies on this page.

Thus, this record is still suitable for explaining why the old investigation started with the RBF cache, but not for declaring current module responsibilities or current bounds behavior. For reports that cannot be linked to an object, a call relationship or a fee check location, stop at the corresponding branch and retain the original issue wording.
