# Duration and CPFP Foreign Key Migration Notes

This page originally did little more than put two names into a compatibility checklist: `rounded until duration` was considered something related to the time component, and `CPFP foreign-key ordering` was simply placed after it. The old checklist kept being brought back into use because it provided a page entry point from which to start investigating; that was also the problem, as the entry point was mistaken for where the implementation belonged.

This migration record is not being retained to turn the old checklist into a new overall guide. It records how a check moved from "look at the page first" to "verify the page and the generated artifacts separately". The two items can still be handled in the same scheduling cycle, but they should no longer share a single conclusions column.

## The Old Workflow Retained for Reference

The following excerpt is the procedure from the first draft, retained because some people still start their search at this address:

```text
Old checklist

rounded until duration
    |
    v
frontend/src/app/components/time/time.component.ts
    |
    +-- StateService
    `-- dates

CPFP foreign-key ordering
    |
    `-- Continue verification from the component entry point above
```

The assumption at the time was: since related names could be found near the time component, the two compatibility items could initially be closed out in the same place. This assumption was useful only for navigation, not for making migration decisions. It did not explain where the files for the CPFP item came from, or whether ordering was determined by the frontend component; much less did it separate "displaying a duration" and "the foreign-key order in generated files" into two verification tracks.

The old checklist's instruction to "Continue verification from the component entry point above" is outdated. It is retained to explain why early follow-up checks stopped at the page code, not to have future maintainers continue following it.

## Page-Side Migration Entry Point

`frontend/src/app/components/time/time.component.ts` remains an available local entry point for working on `rounded until duration`. Dependencies visible in the file include:

```ts
import { Component, OnInit, OnDestroy, ChangeDetectionStrategy, Input, ChangeDetectorRef, OnChanges } from '@angular/core';
import { StateService } from '../../services/state.service';
import { dates } from '../../shared/i18n/dates';
```

These lines help break the old record down into smaller verification steps: first check the time inputs, sources of state, and date terms actually used inside the component; then record the call sites you find under the time item, rather than treating import statements as the behavior itself. `Input`, `OnChanges`, and `ChangeDetectorRef` indicate supporting conditions for this component to receive external values and update when they change, but they do not replace verification of the specific call sites. `dates` likewise only shows that the page has dependencies related to date terms or formatting, and cannot establish the rounding convention on its own.

After migration, the time item's record should use the following format, rather than "covered by the component":

```text
Name: rounded until duration
Starting point: frontend/src/app/components/time/time.component.ts
Call sites found in this check: ________
Source of state or input: ________
Result actually displayed on the page: ________
Callers still requiring follow-up: ________
```

These blanks are not there just to fill out a table. The old record did not provide these values, and later follow-up checks did not add a complete sample here either, so the empty fields must not be filled with guesses. What can be done on the page side is to narrow the search to actual references among the component, state service, and date terms; if a caller does not fall within this scope, do not keep following the old checklist's arrows and force a connection.

In cases where the old page check needs to be restored temporarily, the fallback should likewise be to restore this entry point, not the old assumption that "the two issues share a page component". In other words, you can return to `time.component.ts` to recheck `rounded until duration`, but the CPFP item must remain in a separate column, pending artifact checks. This leaves two unfinished records, but it does not put an unverifiable association back into the compatibility conclusions.

## Separating the CPFP Item from the Page Checklist

The follow-up entry point for `CPFP foreign-key ordering` comes from MEM-226. This item calls not for inspecting the time component, but for rerunning the corresponding entry point on a platform supported by the maintainers and checking the actual generated files and versions. Here, "ordering" is the name of the thing being checked; this page contains no record of what a particular order should look like, and no rules should be supplied based on the name.

The sequence adopted after the split is as follows:

1. First retain the original name of CPFP in the old checklist, to avoid rewriting it as a time-display issue during migration.
2. On a supported platform, go to the corresponding rerun entry point and obtain the actual generated files and the observed versions.
3. Check the files and versions together with this run; if there are no artifacts, record that no artifacts were obtained, rather than substituting page code.
4. When counterexamples are encountered, keep them in the CPFP column, rather than moving them back to the time-component column to explain them.
5. Once the existing branch is complete, hand it over for review to confirm whether it satisfies this check, rather than recording "sent for review" as "the ordering is now correct".

This sequence comes from the work trail left by a later follow-up check: counterexamples were later added to the CPFP item, and it was sent for review after the existing branch was completed. The specifics of the counterexamples are not on this page; their value is in preventing the old checklist from continuing to treat "the component file can be found" as completion of the check. Sending it for review likewise only indicates that the implementation has been submitted for inspection, and cannot replace records of actual checks of the generated files and versions.

Accordingly, the CPFP migration column should retain two types of material: files and versions obtained from reruns, and unresolved counterexamples. Do not reduce the former to "rerun completed", or abstract the latter as "there are edge cases". The actual files, observed versions, and entry points corresponding to the counterexamples are what someone can pick up next time.

```text
CPFP foreign-key ordering

Old entry point: Alongside the time item in the compatibility checklist
New entry point: Corresponding rerun on the maintenance platform
Retained material: Actual generated files, versions, counterexamples
Not a substitute: Page location of time.component.ts
```

The label "Not a substitute" in the diagram above does not mean that the page component is irrelevant, but that it cannot stand in for checking the generated artifacts. The old checklist linked the two because no more detailed entry-point records were available at the time; after the split, both can still begin as part of the same round of compatibility work, but the evidence is no longer mixed together.

## A Check Interrupted by Permissions

MEM-209 was once blocked after a round of release categorization because a standard-permission account had not yet been enabled. This pause needs to be included in the migration record because it explains why the old checklist had a state of "page entry point found" without corresponding verification results.

The fact that the standard-permission account had not been enabled does not mean that `rounded until duration`'s page behavior had been checked, nor does it mean that there were no issues with it. It only interrupted the checks that required that account at the time. When picking this up later, record it separately from code searches: on the code side, verification of the component's calling relationships can continue; once account access is restored, add the results that can only be seen with standard permissions. Do not let the two cancel each other out.

The old checklist downplayed this pause, as though "it can be finished as soon as permissions are enabled". In hindsight, this was not accurate enough: after permissions are enabled, you still need to return to the time item's actual call sites and confirm whether you are examining the same time-display path this time. Without that step, restoring account access will only move the old checklist from "blocked" to "looks ready to close".

To avoid leaving the same gaps again, retain at least the following four lines in the time item's migration notes:

```text
Is the old page entry point still available: ________
Has an account been obtained for the standard-permission check: ________
Call sites verified this time: ________
Do the verification results and the account-based check come from the same path: ________
```

This is not a general pre-release checklist, but a way to fill the gap left by that permissions-related interruption. The last line is especially important: if the page call sites do not match the results under the account, keep them side by side for now, rather than treating them as the same fact just because they share a term.

## Handoff Boundaries Between the Two Records

MEM-209 is used to navigate to routine usage checks for `rounded until duration`; MEM-226 is used to navigate to platform reruns and artifact checks for `CPFP foreign-key ordering`. Both cards can be open at once, but when updating records, do not put one card's status into the other card's conclusions.

For the time item, the handoff material consists of verified call sites near the page component, sources of state, and callers that have not yet been found. For the CPFP item, the handoff material consists of the rerun entry point on the maintenance platform, the actual generated files, the observed versions, and the retained counterexamples. The former is not complete just because the latter has an existing branch, nor is the latter complete just because the former's page path is clear.

DOC-21 records a separate set of verification designs involving `in-sync mempool removal` and a separate audit summary endpoint. It may come up as related material, but do not bring its verification language into this migration table; the only outstanding issues here are the entry point for checking the time display and the ordering check for CPFP artifacts.

## Handling Current References to the Old Checklist

Some links still take readers directly to `time.component.ts`. When encountering such a link, there is no need to rewrite the link text first; first determine which name it points to.

- The link points to `rounded until duration`: Start with the component and add the actual call sites and input sources. If the old note only lists `StateService` or `dates`, treat it as a starting point, not a completion marker.
- The link points to `CPFP foreign-key ordering`: Treat the link as a historical clue, go to the rerun entry point on the maintenance platform, and check the generated files and versions.
- The link does not specify which item: Do not guess based on the component's location. Keep the original link and add the name that needs to be confirmed next to it; do not move it into either column until the name is confirmed.

The recovery procedure in the old records therefore also changes. Previously, if a check could not proceed, it fell back to the same page entry point; now, the time item can return to the page entry point for further investigation, while the CPFP item returns to the rerun entry point to obtain artifacts again. Both recovery paths are more specific than "go back to the old checklist and look again", but they do not create a shared implementation that does not exist.

This page remains migration material from an earlier point in time, and should not be treated as a complete definition of current behavior. It retains the component entry point, an interruption caused by a standard-permission account not being enabled, and the counterexamples and review trail for the CPFP item, and separates the two verification paths that were previously mixed together. The missing caller information for the time item and the detailed file records for the CPFP item still need to be filled in at their respective entry points.

# Worker UID Interface Proposal

This round, we'll try worker UID decoding and detailed projected ranges separately, rather than treating them as two fields in a single interface expansion. The first concerns whether the UID received on the worker side retains a usable interpretation at the interface boundary; the second concerns whether projected data should have a finer-grained representation than the existing ranges. If the two are bundled together, callers will have trouble telling whether a problem comes from a change in identifier interpretation or a change in range representation.

There are two initial options. The first is to interpret UID close to where the worker produces its output, then have the block interface read the processed results. The second is to pass the raw UID through to the interface layer and let the interface handle it based on its own context. The first makes it easier to centralize interpretation, but makes the shape of the worker's output a dependency for downstream callers; the second requires fewer changes to the worker, but could lead to different entry points developing their own interpretations.

For detailed projected ranges, I don't yet recommend assuming they must be incorporated into the existing block object. We can first compare two approaches: "adding detail to the existing object" and "providing a result that only callers needing the details will read." The first saves one read; the second makes it easier to keep range details from bogging down the normal block view. We haven't received any caller samples yet, so we can't determine which approach is more suitable on this basis.

We'll also spell out the backout conditions up front: if UID can't be interpreted to mean the same thing at both entry points, we won't commit to it as a stable part of the interface; if range details require existing block readers to understand a new hierarchy, we'll back out the object extension first and keep the separate-result experiment. What's missing isn't more fields, but an actual read path and its requirements for the shape of the returned data.

# Worker UID Interface Proposal

The previous draft discussed worker UID decoding and detailed projected ranges separately, and the rationale still holds: where UID is interpreted determines who is responsible for ensuring consistent semantics; where the range details are placed determines whether ordinary block readers have to accept a new return shape. The previous draft leaned toward interpreting it on the worker side first and treating the range details as a candidate extension to the existing block object. That was only an assumption to make the initial comparison easier, not a settled interface direction.

Later, a caller follow-up check was added, with the entry recorded at MEM-212. The check shows that how it is consumed cannot be inferred from the interface name alone; the record does not fill in the caller's version, entry point, or actual result, so "there is a caller" cannot be written as "there is already a compatible caller." This gap remains to prevent a walkthrough from later being mistaken for validation.

The source location is still `backend/src/api/mempool-blocks.ts`. Near the top of the file, you can see `logger`, `config`, and `Common`, along with interface types such as `MempoolBlock`, `MempoolBlockWithTransactions`, `MempoolBlockDelta`, `TransactionExtended`, `ThreadTransaction`, `TransactionStripped`, and `Ancestor`. This is enough to serve as an entry point for continued checking, but not enough to prove which layer should interpret UID, or to determine which kind of return object should contain detailed projected ranges.

Accordingly, adjust the trial order: first trace one real read site to confirm whether it receives the worker-processed value or the value assembled by the interface layer; then record separately whether that read site actually needs detailed ranges. If those two answers come from different read sites, do not force them together just to share one change. Range details can remain a candidate result; do not assume they are a fixed component of `MempoolBlock`.

The previous draft's statement that "interpreting first in the worker would be more centralized" should be downgraded. Centralization does not automatically mean clear boundaries: if the interface still needs to add meaning based on block context, the responsibility has not disappeared even if interpretation happens earlier. Conversely, interface-layer handling does not necessarily cause duplication in multiple places, provided the read entry points actually share the same assembly path; this has not been confirmed.

No new fields are recommended in this round. During further trials, if it is found that UID can only be interpreted within a single worker output, stop promoting it as a generic interface value; if detailed projected ranges serve only a small number of readers, prioritize retaining a local return rather than requiring all block readers to migrate. # Worker UID API Proposal

This proposal initially framed the issue as "have the worker decode UID first, then attach the detailed ranges to the block object". That wording made it easy to plan a small change, but collapsed two boundaries into one: worker UID decoding concerns where UID is given an interpretation usable by the API; detailed projected ranges concerns who requests the details of projection results and the shape in which they are returned. Some later readers have continued to use that old conclusion, so the original assessment is retained, but is no longer treated as the default implementation path.

In the old proposal, the worker was responsible for first normalizing UID into a stable identity, and the API read the normalized value; the range portion directly extended the existing block object. The advantage was that callers appeared to need only one read. The costs were not made clear at the time: if UID carries meaning that holds only in the API context, normalizing it in advance does not amount to completing its interpretation; and if range details are used by only a few readers, putting them in a public object forces readers that do not care about those details to deal with a new object hierarchy as well. The old draft contains no call results and cannot prove that these costs have already occurred; it can only show that they were not ruled out at the time.

Now that MEM-212 has been supplemented with caller_walkthrough, the earlier assessment that "finding the API entry point is enough to confirm compatibility" should be withdrawn. The walkthrough itself is not an API example, nor does it record the caller's actual version, job entry point, or results. It can narrow subsequent checks to an existing automation entry point, but cannot replace inspection of the returned object. Anyone following up from this page should first add the job's commit and actual artifact name to MEM-212, rather than directly using the old draft's preference as the basis for a change.

For UID, there are still three options for assigning responsibility to compare.

- Have the worker output an interpreted UID, with the API only forwarding it. This remains the shortest read path, but requires the interpretation in the worker's output to cover all API read contexts.
- The worker retains the raw UID, and the `mempool-blocks` side interprets it using local context. This avoids prematurely fixing a common meaning for the worker's output, but requires confirmation that different APIs will not each develop their own set of rules.
- The API only passes through UID, leaving interpretation to callers. This can reduce server-side changes, but distributes interpretation of the same UID across callers; unless callers can be shown to already have a consistent convention, it should not be treated as the default approach.

No option is selected here. The old draft's "worker interprets first" approach is retained only as a candidate and is no longer presented as a recommendation. The next sample should answer a very specific question: whether the read point needs a directly displayable UID, or a UID that still requires assessment in light of the block or projection state. The former result supports placing interpretation as close to the output as possible; the latter indicates that the API layer must at least retain responsibility for interpretation. If the sample covers only one worker output, the result cannot be generalized to all entry points either.

The range portion also needs to be resolved separately. Detailed ranges may be additional content in the existing `MempoolBlock` view, or may need to be fetched separately by readers interested only in projection details. The old draft treated "one fewer read" as the main reason to extend the object, but that reason is too weak: eliminating one read does not offset the migration cost of requiring all callers to accept the returned shape. Conversely, separate results are not inherently safer either; they introduce additional issues around read ordering and result pairing. Until there are actual callers, both paths are only candidates.

For now, the following criteria can keep the trial scope bounded: only if detailed ranges are indispensable to ordinary block reads should the costs of incorporating them into the block object be compared; if they appear only in dedicated projection checks, keep the results local for now. This assessment does not require deciding on the final field names first, nor does it require putting UID and the range changes in the same commit. The two can share a round of verification, but not a release commitment.

`backend/src/api/mempool-blocks.ts` remains the source-code entry point for this record. The visible `MempoolBlock`, `MempoolBlockWithTransactions`, and `MempoolBlockDelta` indicate that this code at least sits alongside several block-result shapes; `TransactionExtended`, `ThreadTransaction`, `TransactionStripped`, and `Ancestor` are a reminder not to mistake the "block object" for the only representation of a transaction during review. `Common`, `config`, and `logger` appear in the same file header, but the existing record does not establish a specific relationship between them and UID decoding or range details, so implementation responsibilities should not be assigned on that basis.

Responsibility boundaries are therefore described by object rather than by filename for now: the candidate owners for worker UID decoding are the side that produces the interpretation of UID and the side that exposes that interpretation; the candidate owners for detailed projected ranges are the side that maintains the projection shape and the side that consumes those details. The API owner needs to make the final decision on the public shape, and the core implementation side needs to provide a snippet showing where the actual data is obtained; until then, any claim that it is "already guaranteed by the worker" or "already handled uniformly by the API" is just an old assumption.

MEM-229 can be used to find callers that still use detailed projected ranges and record their actual versions, entry points, and current results. It should not be merged with MEM-212 into a generalized verification checklist: the former answers whether range details are needed, while the latter preserves clues to the automation entry point related to UID. If a caller has confirmed only the ranges and not UID, this round can still move forward with just the ranges; the reverse is also true.

The exception boundaries adjacent to indexed clock modes and full-RBF audit classification are not addressed in this proposal, see DOC-24 separately. The withdrawal conditions here remain twofold: when UID cannot be interpreted consistently in the target read context, do not commit to it as a general-purpose API value; when range details require ordinary block readers to handle irrelevant levels of hierarchy, do not incorporate them into the public block object. The old draft still has reference value because it records why the changes were originally intended to be combined; however, anyone citing it should read it together with this correction.

# WebSocket State Compatibility Notes

When this page was first written, the troubleshooting record contained only a string of easily confused terms: websocket, state, updates, keys, null, json, property. They led readers to `backend/src/api/websocket-handler.ts`, but did not explain which were search clues and which were objects in the code. That record still has value because it preserved the old entry point; however, the string of terms itself can no longer be treated as a compatibility conclusion.

This check continues to use `internal/MEM`'s `v_prev` as the old path. Here, the "old path" is neither an old protocol version nor a production rollback plan, but a reading path from historical issue names and call names back to the source code. To begin, you only need to locate one file:

```text
backend/src/api/websocket-handler.ts
```

The adjacencies shown at the top of the file are enough for a first stop:

```ts
import logger from '../logger';
import * as WebSocket from 'ws';
import blocks from './blocks';
```

Here, `logger`, `ws`, and `blocks` are visible direct dependencies. They show why reading cannot stop at snippets with state in their names: log output, WebSocket types or objects, and block-side objects may all appear in the local context of the same file. An import declaration that has not been expanded is also visible at the top of the file; this record does not add its source or purpose.

The situation before and after migration can be understood as follows:

```text
Old troubleshooting record
  Issue names / Call names / Scattered search terms
              |
              v
backend/src/api/websocket-handler.ts @ v_prev
              |
              v
Confirm state-related, initialization, and update snippets one by one

Post-migration check record
  Pinned version + File entry point + Search term locations
              |
              v
Save terminal output and workspace side effects separately
              |
              v
Decide whether to continue tracing to callers relevant to compatibility
```

The last step in the diagram does not mean expanding every check into a full-repository read. Here, callers relevant to compatibility means code locations that directly depend on or reach this WebSocket handler entry point. Only proceed to the caller side after confirming in the current file that a state snippet is actually used externally; if you are still working from search results, write only "Candidate location identified" in the record, and do not judge the state format to be compatible or incompatible.

## Practices Retained from the Old Record

The following content comes from the initial draft. It is retained so that later maintainers know where the work started, not because it is sufficient to complete the check.

1. Pin the version being read. The old record points to `v_prev`; do not retroactively apply code snippets from later branches to this entry point.
2. Use names to locate code first. `websocket`, `state`, `updates`, `keys`, `null`, `json`, and `property` can still be used to narrow the reading scope.
3. Save outputs separately. Terminal output captured from a local run and side effects in the workspace after that run are not the same type of material. The former helps check what was seen when the behavior was triggered, while the latter helps identify whether any additional content was written or generated.

The initial draft phrased the third point as "Keeping both is enough to finish." That statement no longer applies. Having both types of material only means that the runtime evidence has been recorded; it cannot replace checking state objects and call locations one by one.

## The Actual Order for Migrating Away from the Old Entry Point

First open the target file in the pinned version; do not start by searching the entire repository for `json` or `null`. These two terms are too broad. Starting with a global search will return many unrelated locations and make the old record look as though it describes a general serialization convention. The correct order is to search within the target file first, then decide whether to expand the scope based on the context.

The first pass is only for locating code; do not modify any code or configuration.

- When you find a snippet adjacent to WebSocket initialization, note whether it is part of initialization, message sending, state assembly, or a logging path; do not classify it as state logic merely because it is next to the `WebSocket` import.
- When you find `state`, distinguish whether it is an object name, a property name, a word in a comment, or plain text. The old troubleshooting record did not preserve this distinction.
- When you find `updates` or `keys`, retain a short excerpt before and after it that provides enough context to identify its role, and do not treat the number of search matches as the number of calls.
- When you find `null`, record which local expression it appears in. It may indicate a missing value, or it may simply be a control path unrelated to state; do not make a migration judgment without context.
- When you find `json` or `property`, likewise first determine whether they are adjacent to WebSocket state. Having the same name does not mean they are the same object.

Only in the second pass should you look for connections between these snippets. Here, connections means data passing, initialization order, or message assembly relationships that can be read directly within the same file, not an architecture diagram guessed from module names. If a snippet is only adjacent to `logger`, record it as logging adjacency; if a snippet appears only in the context of `blocks`, record only block-side adjacency. Do not force the three adjacencies together just to complete a state flow diagram.

Only in the third pass should you decide whether to examine callers. The conditions are simple: a local object related to serialized websocket state is already identifiable in the target file, and you need to confirm how external entry points use it. If these two conditions are not met, stop within the file and record the specific gap. For example, "Found a text match for state, but have not confirmed whether it feeds into message updates" is more useful than "Call relationships remain to be investigated," because it tells the next person where to continue.

## Batching the Compatibility Check

This time, do not put all the historical terms into a single pass. The only purpose of batching is to avoid mixing location, interpretation, and run results.

**Batch 1: Entry point and version.**

Confirm that the file being read is `backend/src/api/websocket-handler.ts`, and that the content belongs to `v_prev`. The old record leads here from issue names and call names, so this file is the starting point, not the confirmed sole implementation location. If you have opened another revision, stop first, switch back to the pinned version, and only then take notes; changes in text or imports between versions can cause the old search terms to lose their reference points.

**Batch 2: State terms within the file.**

Check the old terms one by one, but record only the first confirmed context for each term, once. There is no requirement to list all matches or interpret every term as a field. The goal is a brief local record: which term appears near initialization, which appears near updates, and which is merely unrelated text. Leave matches without enough context blank; do not fill them in with guesses.

**Batch 3: Initialization and updates.**

The unresolved question left by the initial draft was "Do properties added during initialization and regular updates go through the same state assembly code?" This question should remain, but it needs to be narrower: first confirm whether properties added during initialization are visible in the target file; then confirm whether regular updates are visible; only then compare whether the two share a local assembly process. If anything required by these steps cannot be located in the pinned version, do not conclude that they are shared or separate.

**Batch 4: Runtime evidence.**

When running "serialized websocket state" through the user's usual entry point, save terminal output and workspace side effects separately. Do not mix later manual annotations into the former; do not substitute terminal text for the latter. If there are no discernible changes before and after the run, faithfully record "No discernible changes observed," and do not reinterpret the source code merely because nothing changed. The run only supplements runtime evidence; it must not override local relationships already identified in the file.

## Record Format

Each review only needs to leave a few lines that the next pass can use. The following format can be used; leave the contents of square brackets blank when unconfirmed rather than filling them with speculation.

```text
Pinned version: v_prev
File entry point: backend/src/api/websocket-handler.ts
Search term: state
Location: [Initialization / Update / Other / Unconfirmed]
Adjacent objects: [logger / WebSocket / blocks / Other local objects]
Caller side: Not examined / Examined but unconfirmed / Location confirmed
Terminal output: Saved / Missing
Workspace side effects: Saved / Missing
Conclusion for this pass: [Location only / Ready for further comparison / Return to the old entry point required]
```

"Location confirmed" may only be entered after reading an explicit call or usage relationship. Do not treat finding a filename in a search, a successful build, or a terminal run with no errors as confirmation of the caller side. Conversely, if a state term appears in the target file but you do not yet know who uses it, simply enter "Not examined"; this is not a failure, just the limit of this pass's scope.

## When to Return to the Old Entry Point

Returning does not modify WebSocket, nor does it attempt to restore state to an old value. It only resets the checking process: return to the pinned version, target file, and original search terms, and rebuild a minimal record.

Return in the following situations:

- Runtime output and workspace side effects were mixed into the same record, and their respective sources can no longer be distinguished.
- You jumped to content outside `v_prev` while reading, but have already included those observations in this check.
- You started with a global search that returned many matches for `json`, `null`, or `property`, and can no longer explain which came from the target file.
- You recorded conclusions about calls based on imports, similar names, or directory locations without having read a direct relationship.

The first record after returning does not require redoing the entire investigation. Simply pin the entry point again, write down the terms and locations that can currently be confirmed, and then decide whether to rerun for runtime evidence. The issue names and call names in the old record can still serve as navigation; they no longer serve as conclusions.

## Addendum to This Review

MEM-214 was marked as reviewed in a subsequent documentation review. The card still has one unchecked item: run "serialized websocket state" through the user's usual entry point, and save terminal output and workspace side effects separately. This is consistent with the migration order on this page, but the card is not the source of the state format definition; it only provides an entry point for continuing to collect runtime evidence.

This pass did not add any verifiable field table, nor did it define `updates`, `keys`, `null`, or `property` as a fixed JSON structure. The target file's local dependencies and the old search terms can support the next reading, but are not enough to replace checking each location. In particular, the relationship between "properties added during initialization" and "regular updates" should still be handled in the order given in Batch 3.

If external usage locations are actually identified in a later reading, simply append them to the record for the corresponding search term; there is no need to rewrite the first half of this page. If you discover that the old record classified unrelated matches as part of the state path, retain the old entries and note beside them that they have been corrected; this will still explain why the work originally started from this entry point. DOC-26 can serve as navigation for related verification design, but do not include the objects covered by its statistics in this WebSocket state check.

# Quality Signal Window Closeout Operations Checklist

Closing the window does not mean cleaning up immediately after the page turns green. For this round, the quality signal desk collects only four things: the resources borrowed by the current entry point, the final output, the return time, and the rollback entry for adj-frontend. All other release decisions remain with their respective maintainers.

This page begins with two field reminders from the old version: after seeing `block template`, do not clear the environment; when `socket fallback` does not appear, do not use continued operation to manufacture a conclusion. Later checks showed that what is most easily lost is the revision before clearing the cache or switching the worker, along with the partial state left behind when the exit entry is not completed. Therefore, the closeout order has been changed to preserve a record first, exit second, and return resources last.

Before the window ends, there is no requirement to put all pages into the same state. What is required is that the next person taking over can see which revision this round started from, what was temporarily borrowed, what the last output that was not cleaned up was, and exactly where the rollback action stopped. If any of the four items is blank, the window record should remain incomplete rather than using a single success prompt to fill it in.

## The Line to Write When Opening the Window

Each time a window starts, first write one line in the original record: the current revision, the borrowed resource, the start time, and the latest return window. The borrowed resource can be an account, workspace, worker, environment, or proxy; if nothing was borrowed, write "no temporary resources" and do not omit this item. This lets closeout distinguish between "nothing to return" and "forgot to register it."

- [ ] The current revision was recorded before clearing the cache, switching the worker, or changing the environment.
- [ ] The borrower and return window were written back to the original card.
- [ ] One first-visible output has been retained for the current entry point.
- [ ] If there are no temporary resources in this round, the original record explicitly says so rather than leaving it blank.

MEMA-006 correspond to recording the revision before a cold start. This only addresses whether the baseline was recorded; it does not replace the exit check. If only part of the state is visible at the time, record the visible part and stop guessing; output obtained from later runs cannot be backfilled as the baseline from before startup. Anyone preparing to clear the cache should first check whether this line exists, because once the cache is cleared, the revision that was previously visible cannot be recovered from memory.

MEMA-009 are the registration entry for the resource return window. This item was previously handled separately and was later merged into the maintenance card for the same module; the return information on the page still needs to be written clearly. The borrowing time must not be hidden in chat just because the card is no longer handled independently. After the registration item is merged, the closeout record still needs to retain the borrowed resource and the latest return window so that the person taking over can verify them one by one.

## Retain the First Result

A window may produce a success path or a rejection path. Keep one sample of each, and retain the original input, the current revision, and the result seen the first time in each sample. Here, "sample" refers only to the result left by this quality signal desk check; it does not require additional runs for every scenario.

Save the final output first, then discuss whether to clean up the temporary state. When `block template` appears, save the state before and after it; it cannot by itself prove that the subsequent exit has completed. `template persistence` is a locator term used in the old checklist. It can still be used to find the check location at that time, but it should not be treated as a release condition. After seeing this marker, return to the revision, output, and exit action for this round rather than treating a locator term as a complete result.

- [ ] The first result from this round is retained for the success path.
- [ ] The first result from this round and the stopping point are retained for the rejection path.
- [ ] The final output was saved before cleanup.
- [ ] Any account, workspace, cache, or worker changed for diagnosis is marked separately.

When temporary diagnostics have changed the environment, the green page that appears again after cleanup cannot overwrite the first result. The changed result may remain in the same round's record, but it must be written separately from the first result to avoid misreading "what can be seen after switching the workspace" as the result from the original entry point. There is no requirement here to judge which of the two is better; only the changes that actually occurred need to be recorded.

If `socket fallback` does not appear, stop the closeout check here. It is not a prompt for the person on duty to continue switching environments, and even less is it a signal that allows stored output to be deleted. Leave the fact that it did not appear and the position reached. If the account, workspace, or worker has already been changed at this point, mark that beside the stopping point as well, so that a later handler does not treat different environments as the same check.

## The Two Stopping Points at the Exit Entry

Rollback must be checked by tracing the actual adj-frontend back through the exit action. The filename, page color, or a single success prompt cannot replace this step. MEMA-012 serve as the entry for this recheck: when closing the window, check the object that the exit action ultimately reached, not a page whose name merely looks similar.

Two failure samples have already been seen, and their handling differs from "try again":

1. After changing the account or workspace, stop upon reaching the exit entry. Retain the current revision before and after the change, the final output, and the stopping point. Do not mark the resource as returned just because the entry point was switched.
2. From the normal entry, inspect the exit entry and get rejected at the second step. This means that the normal entry is insufficient to complete the check. Record where the rejection occurred and stop there; do not repeatedly switch the normal entry to create more contradictory results.

Neither of these samples is evidence that rollback succeeded. They also do not mean that the exit entry itself is unavailable; they only mean that this check was not completed. The closeout record should explicitly say "not verified" rather than "expected to have been rolled back." When the check needs to continue, the person taking over should start from the stopping point rather than re-evaluating based on the previous round's page color.

- [ ] The exit action was rechecked against the actual adj-frontend.
- [ ] If the entry was rejected, the rejection location and previous output were saved, and further attempts were stopped.
- [ ] If the process remained stopped after changing the account or workspace, the resource still being borrowed and the return window were recorded.
- [ ] The page result from the normal entry was not treated as confirmation that rollback was complete.

When the exit action moves beyond the current entry point, the checklist's responsibility ends here. The original record should retain the current revision, the final output, and the point where it moved beyond the entry; this information lets the next maintainer continue the verification and avoids changing the environment one more time just to complete a closeout form. This page does not decide the steps beyond the interface on their behalf.

## Handling Before and After the Due Time

Returning resources is not a task to do casually at the end of the window. First compare the registered latest return window, then confirm whether the exit action has been completed; only when both match can the resource be crossed off the record for this round. The fact that one item has been returned does not mean that the other temporary resources on the same line have also been returned.

MEMA-015 are used to verify the publication time of adj-frontend and the rollback entry for the old value. Recently, there have been cases where the person on duty was offline and nobody was temporarily available to verify the due-time action. In this situation, do not write waiting as completed: retain the old value as a rollback entry that remains available, note in the original record that the due-time action has not yet been verified, and keep the revision, borrowed resource, and final output needed for handoff together.

The purpose of retaining the old value is that the rollback entry remains usable, not to grant default permission to delay cleanup. As long as the exit action is still stopped at the rejection from the normal entry, or the account or workspace was changed but the process still did not complete, the old value cannot be treated as proof that the replacement has been completed. Writing "not yet verified" in the record is more useful than writing a completed state that cannot be rechecked.

- [ ] There is someone available to verify the due-time action, or the original record is clearly marked as not yet verified.
- [ ] The old value remains until the rollback entry has been fully rechecked.
- [ ] The temporary account, workspace, worker, environment, and proxy have been individually confirmed as returned; if only one of them is confirmed, do not mark the entire item complete.
- [ ] The temporary state for this round is cleared only after the queue is no longer accepting new work.

If the return window has arrived while the exit entry is still unverified, retain both of the following in the record: the registered return time for the resource and the actual stopping point of the rollback action. Do not delete the stopping point because the time has arrived, and do not rewrite the registered return window because the entry was not completed. The two items describe the resource agreement and the operation progress separately; omitting either one will deprive later decisions of their basis.

## Minimum Form of the Window Closeout Record

A normal round's closeout can be as short as four lines:

- The current revision has been recorded;
- The final output has been saved;
- The return window for the temporary resources has been verified;
- The exit entry has been rechecked, or the stopping point has been stated explicitly.

If any of the four lines is missing, do not cover it with "window ended." Especially when rollback fails, retaining the old value and the original sample is more important than arranging a complete page.

Related entries: MEMA-006 record the revision baseline, MEMA-009 record the borrowing and return window, MEMA-012 are used to recheck the exit action, and MEMA-015 are used to verify the publication time and the rollback entry for the old value.

# Quality Signal Cache Trade-off Decision

The cache for frontend-quality-signal and the original live state were considered together in the same trade-off at the time. The choice was between continuing along `mined conflict` and splitting `replacement tree` out separately. The failure exit is different in each case: the former continues on the existing path, while the latter leaves the replacement tree's failure isolated. That difference is the direct reason for retaining the current revision. If the environment were rebuilt first, the state in the original setup would be mixed with the rebuilt state, making it difficult to determine later which change caused a failure.

Decision: retain the current revision and do not make rebuilding the environment a prerequisite; structurally, use a separate `replacement tree`. Here, "separate" limits only the boundary of the record and the evaluation; it does not mean the new tree has already been wired into all callers, nor that the old entry point has become permanent. The current revision is the state on which this decision relies; freezing it first preserves the comparison conditions better than cleaning up the environment first.

The objections were not removed. The active callers of `worker snapshot` had not been determined at the time, and who would take over this call after the split had also not been decided; it was likewise undecided whether the rollback would restore only the old entry point. These are later choices about integration and exit actions, and are not enough to overturn this structural decision. Results from later exit actions should be appended to this record and must not be written back as facts known in v1. # Dependency Boundary Dual-State Issue Postmortem

This incident left behind not a failed command, but two audit records that both appeared to be "current". They describe the same set of dependency sources formed by lock and license: the scopes that use them, who maintains them, and which entry point must be used when exiting. The object itself has its own schedule and exit conditions, so when the two states coexist, they cannot be handled as a routine cache refresh, nor can either record be chosen first as the baseline for subsequent checks.

The old record is still at `docs/adj-backend/incidents/backend-dependency-boundary-audit-same-object-appears-in-two-states.md`. The initial version only noted that the replacement tree differed from the old record and preserved the inputs used at the time. Restoring the worker snapshot later made it possible to retrieve the earlier incident state; however, the restoration did not also reveal why the transaction cluster had changed. The decision in the initial version to stop further retries was correct: the full command arguments were unavailable then, and repeated execution would only have produced a third result with no context annotations.

## Impact

The impact was on the validity of comparing dependency boundary audits, not on any confirmed removal or renewed adoption of a particular source. The two points in time showed different current revisions, so none of the following could be established directly at the time:

- Whether the old record still represented the same environment;
- Whether the scope of adoption of a lock or license source had changed;
- Whether the exit action applied to the original set of sources or the later set;
- Whether the branch handed off to the maintainer actually started from the same entry point.

The incident record therefore retained the original record, the restored page, and the fact that the cause remained unconfirmed. The restored state only shows that one path is visible again, not that the two audit states have converged. Previously, someone had treated the last successful output as the conclusion, but that judgment was not reused this time: without the full arguments accompanying the output, there is no way to know which current revision it corresponds to.

## Timeline Added Later

| Time | Record | What could be concluded at the time |
|---|---|---|
| Initial discovery | replacement tree differs from the old record | Neither record can overwrite the other; preserve the original inputs first. |
| After restoring the incident state | worker snapshot can be restored | The original state can be reviewed, but the reason for the transaction cluster change is still unknown. |
| Month 1, day 26 | MEMB-010 pinned the toolchain | The toolchain was pinned; subsequent comparisons should not introduce toolchain drift. |
| Month 1, day 27 | MEMB-010 began handling the issue | The last output still needs to be saved before exit; the work is not yet complete. |
| Month 1, day 28 | MEMB-009 checked rollback; MEMB-013 checked dependencies | Rollback and dependency-side conditions have been checked, but the dual state is still unexplained. |
| Month 1, day 29 | The two environments show different current results | The command has not yet been recovered; environmental differences need to be listed separately and cannot be attributed directly to the source set. |
| Later that day | The current result appeared only under cold-cache conditions | The expiration action still shows the original result; the cold-cache behavior does not prove that the exit entry point has been executed. |

The easiest things to confuse in the timeline are "the result reappeared" and "the states are comparable". The current result appearing under cold-cache conditions shows that this condition changes the visible output; the expiration action still showing the original result shows that the two observations have not naturally merged into a single state. Putting them on the same line would give the false impression that the old result was no longer valid. Both observations are retained here, each labeled with the conditions under which it occurred.

When the two environments produced different current results, the original command had not been recovered. This gap limits the comparisons that can be made: one result cannot be used to infer the other environment's dependency sources, adoption scope, or exit responsibilities. MEMB-009 recorded that the original command arguments were missing; any arguments recovered later should be logged in a separate record rather than backfilled into the initial incident record, to avoid presenting later inputs as inputs already used at the time.

## Boundaries for On-Call Handling

The handling in MEMB-010 separated "preserving state" from "releasing state". Before releasing the current revision, the exit code, the contents of this dependency boundary audit, and the final log section should be preserved. The aim is not to save a full copy of every run, but to associate the exit action with the audit state that preceded it. Without these three items, the next green result can only show that that run ended, not that it was under the same comparison conditions as the old record.

Before switching environments, MEMB-012 required exporting the current audit and exit action. After the switch, the old and new sides are no longer described as a comparison within the same round. This restriction follows directly from this dual-state incident: if the environment, cache conditions, or current revision is not held fixed, the result can only be treated as a new observation. This does not mean that all environmental differences are root causes; the existing records do not establish that.

The comparison method agreed on in MEMB-013 is narrower: hold backend-supply-boundary, the current entry point, and the command fixed, and change only the current revision. The aim here is not to revalidate the entire dependency system, but to determine whether the revision alone is sufficient to explain the two audit states. This comparison cannot begin while the command is still missing; manually approximated arguments should not be substituted for the original command and their output then recorded as an official comparison result.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Saved old audit record] --> B{Is the current entry point the same}
    B -- No --> C[Archive as a new observation]
    B -- Yes --> D{Can the command and environment be confirmed}
    D -- No --> E[Retain both states, do not compare adoption scope]
    D -- Yes --> F[Hold the boundary and command fixed]
    F --> G[Change only the current revision]
    G --> H{Has the exit action been executed}
    H -- No --> I[Do not treat the cold-cache result as the exit result]
    H -- Yes --> J[Record the exit code and final log section]
```

The diagram's "same current entry point" refers only to this audit's entry point. It does not require other systems to reuse the same criteria. For this incident, the branch after the entry point has been handed to the current maintainer for further handling; MEMB-011 records that backend-supply-boundary is usable, but this does not confirm the root cause of the dual state.

## Rejected Attributions

Initial suspicion fell on the replacement tree itself: it was the first to diverge from the old record, and on the surface this looked much like a change to the source set. After the worker snapshot was restored, this explanation was insufficient to account for the incident state. The snapshot made the old state visible again, but did not explain the change in the transaction cluster; later observations included different results in the two environments, the current result appearing only under cold-cache conditions, and the expiration action still showing the original result. The available material better supports treating the replacement tree as the first place where the anomaly was discovered, rather than as a confirmed cause.

Another premature conclusion was "the user path is restored, so the issue is over". The restored page was not treated here as evidence that the root cause had been resolved. The restoration only shows that the worker snapshot retained at the time can be retrieved again; it did not provide the full command or establish whether the exit entry point had finished running. The on-call handling in MEMB-010 was only half complete, and the subsequent exit entry point was not executed, which means the time of restoration and the time of exit completion must be recorded separately.

Rollback checks likewise did not yield a conclusion that would allow the incident to be closed. The rollback check in MEMB-009 means that the rollback path was examined, not that rollback caused the two states or that all audit records became consistent again after rollback. The dependency check result also only confirms that the check took place; it cannot replace a controlled comparison of the environment, command, and revision.

## Retention Approach

Do not overwrite the original record or the restored page. Alongside each, retain the observation conditions: the known current revision, whether the cache was cold, whether the environment was switched, and whether the exit action was completed; if the full command is missing, state that explicitly. This lets subsequent maintainers viewing the same object first distinguish whether they are looking at the old record, the restored incident state, or a new environmental observation, rather than stitching the three sources into a single continuous log.

Exit-related materials continue to be handled in DOC-36; this page retains only the account of why the two states could not be merged during this incident. Related navigation includes MEMB-009, MEMB-010, MEMB-011, MEMB-012 and MEMB-013.

## Outstanding Items

1. Recover the full command corresponding to each of the two environments and log them separately from the original observations.
2. After holding backend-supply-boundary, the current entry point, and the command fixed, rerun the comparison, changing only the current revision.
3. Complete the exit entry point that was left unfinished during the on-call shift, then record its exit code and final log section.
4. The change in the transaction cluster still has no confirmed explanation; until comparable inputs are available, do not attribute it to the replacement tree, the cache, or an environment switch.

# Dependency Boundary Exit Window Checklist

This checklist still covers the early backend-supply-boundary exit window. The entry point remains at `docs/adj-backend/release/backend-supply-boundary-exit-window-checklist.md`. It is still referenced because several checks have needed to revisit the exit actions and states recorded at the time; it is not a standard procedure for all subsequent release windows.

The original approach was simple: once the last visible result appeared, mark the window as closed. That criterion was retained in version 1, not deleted. Later, the issue was not whether a result had appeared, but whether it actually came from this round's exit action and whether the action hit the actual adj-backend. Version 2 therefore added a reverse check; this version only adds the leads already available from the cards to the check sequence and does not extend to other projects' release policies.

Before starting, review the original record alongside the materials for this round:

- [ ] The exit action must point to a specific object. The method proposed in MEMB-005 is to trace back from the action to the actual adj-backend, not infer it from filenames or page colors.
- [ ] Record the state before the action. The requirement recorded in MEMB-006 is to first export the states from before and after the failure, so do not save only the final page.
- [ ] If a rerun in another environment is needed, keep the source code and commands unchanged, and record the revision at the time. The single-environment failure reproduction in MEMB-007 was recorded within this scope.
- [ ] Separate the exit actions this round is responsible for from other release actions. Only the exit actions for adj-backend are covered here; the relevant owner signs off separately on whether the release succeeded.

During execution, record in this order: "action—object hit—state before and after—last visible result". # Performance Lab Dual-State Postmortem

This record begins with the Performance Lab for contributors. The Performance Lab establishes a capacity baseline for contributors, reviews resource curves, and localizes regressions when deviations appear. It has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, so what is preserved here is an anomaly affecting this work item, not a rewritten account of the overall status of other projects.

On the surface, the anomaly was simple: the current entry point returned different current revision values at two points in time. The object name had not changed, and both checks still went through the same current entry point, so it was initially easy to treat the difference as part of a natural change after a refresh. Only when the incident materials were organized later did it become clear that this wording conflated three different things: "the entry point is accessible," "the entry point points to the same record," and "the two checks belong to the same round of comparison."

The draft preserved only the first divergence and one missing timestamp. This was not because the cause had already been found, but because the saved materials were only sufficient to show that the values seen in the two checks differed. The published version retains this starting point and does not retroactively revise it based on the later recovery result.

## Incident Scope

This anomaly concerns the current entry point used when reviewing the capacity baseline, resource curves, and regression localization. The known difference was in the current revision returned by the entry point. No materials indicate that all Performance Lab work failed at the same moment, nor do any materials indicate that the capacity baseline, resource curves, and regression localization each experienced the same problem.

Therefore, the scope of impact cannot be expanded indefinitely based on the four-character label "Performance Lab anomaly." This name only identifies the work area to which the incident belongs. What was actually preserved was the same object presenting different states at two observation points, and the fact that this prevented the original comparison from continuing as the same round.

The Performance Lab is not merely a read-only directory label. It has an independent schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria; routine reviews discuss the capacity baseline, resource curves, and regression localization together. This incident did not prove that these work items caused changes in one another. It only showed that the comparison entry point they jointly relied on could no longer be treated as a stable backdrop.

This account does not turn "the two revision values differ" into "the record was overwritten." Overwriting was only one possible explanation that might have come to mind at the time. A change to the entry point itself, different comparison conditions for the two checks, the old record and the later entry point not sharing the same source, or additional intermediate states that were not saved have not been ruled out. Prematurely naming any one of these as the cause would undermine the meaning of the original discrepancy that was preserved.

## Initial Incident Snapshot

When the issue was first discovered, the old record already existed, and the current entry point was accessible. When the two were compared, the current revision returned by the entry point differed from the old record. Rather than continuing to check repeatedly in pursuit of a consistent result, the original input and the entry-point version at that time were saved first.

Stopping further retries was a choice made for this incident, not a permanent operating rule. Once the two values differed, each new check would produce another candidate state; even if a later check showed an available state, it could not supply the information missing from the first comparison at the time. What needed to be preserved from the incident was "what was seen the first time," not as many subsequent results as possible.

The location of the original record has not changed: `docs/adj-contributors/incidents/contributors-performance-lab-same-object-appears-in-two-states.md`. This location retains the record from that time, as well as the entry-point version and the recovery page saved separately later. Keeping all three together lets readers return to the initial divergence rather than seeing only an organized final result.

The initial incident snapshot did not include the complete command arguments. This is a specific gap, not a generic lack of "sufficient information." If the arguments are recovered later, they become supplemental materials; even if the supplemental result happens to match the earliest result, it cannot be written back into the initial incident snapshot as though those arguments had been saved from the start. Original observations and observations added later must remain separate.

Complete timestamps between the two checks are also missing. The existing records can establish that different current revision values appeared in sequence, but they are insufficient to show whether there were other entry-point states in between. This gap was retained in the draft and is still not filled in as a continuous timeline in the published version.

## How the Records Are Separated

The incident materials include the original record, the entry-point version, and the recovery page. These are not three names for the same material.

The original record answers: what was seen during the first comparison. It preserves the observation that the two values differed, along with the boundary established by not continuing to retry at that time. The original record cannot prove where the change came from, nor does later recovery of the path invalidate it.

The entry-point version answers: where the comparison began. It allows later checks to return to the current entry point referenced at that time, without blending the old record, the current entry point, and supplemental results into a secondhand account with no traceable source. The entry-point version is not itself an explanation of the cause; it only preserves the comparison location.

The recovery page answers: whether a usable path existed later. The recovery page can show that a particular path had recovered by the time of a subsequent check, but it is not responsible for explaining the initial divergence. Overwriting the original record with the recovery page would lead readers to mistake the anomaly for nothing more than an old state that had already been replaced.

These three materials are retained side by side precisely because the strength of their conclusions differs. The original record supports the narrowest conclusion: there were different values at that time. The entry-point version also supports a narrow conclusion: the comparison began here at that time. The recovery page's conclusion is similarly limited: a particular path was usable later. No one of these materials independently connects all three conclusions into a confirmed causal chain.

Early retellings tended to treat the last usable result as evidence that the incident had ended. This approach was not adopted. The recovery time can be recorded, but it cannot automatically replace the end of the impact window; if the current entry point may still return an old value, path recovery and entry-point consistency are two different states.

## Known Sequence

| Relative order | Preserved observation | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| First comparison | The current entry point and the old record gave different current revision values | Saved the original input and entry-point version, and stopped further retries |
| Subsequent organization | The original record, entry-point version, and recovery page were retained separately | Did not overwrite the initial observation with the recovery result |
| Follow-up retracing | Confirmed only as far as the current entry point | Branches not reproduced remained marked for investigation |
| Pre-publication review | Complete timestamps between the two checks were missing, and the initial arguments were still missing | Retained the gaps rather than filling them with speculation |

The sequence in the table is not a precise clock. The draft already retained the "missing timestamp," and the published version does not disguise relative order as specific dates or run numbers. What can be confirmed is that the comparison showing different values came first, followed by saving the materials and retracing the path; what cannot be confirmed is whether other entry-point states occurred between the two checks.

The first comparison is the stopping point for this postmortem. After different current revision values were found, obtaining more output would not automatically increase the credibility of the initial observation. Instead, it could cause a later state to be mistaken for the original state. Saving the original input and entry-point version preserved a comparison starting point that could still be identified later.

During the subsequent organization, the recovery page was not absorbed into the original record. This allows two facts to coexist: the anomalous state occurred; a particular path was usable later. Neither cancels out the other, nor do they naturally imply the same cause.

The follow-up retracing had a very limited scope. Following the original input, the person retracing the path could confirm only as far as the current entry point, did not reproduce unrecorded branches, and did not supply the missing arguments from the initial incident snapshot. This result can be described as "the entry point is still reachable," but it cannot be elevated to "the anomaly has been fully reproduced" or "all branches have been checked."

The pre-publication review did not fill the old gaps. There were not enough continuous records between the two different values, and the complete arguments had not been saved. Stating these gaps explicitly is more useful than splicing a later check back into the initial incident snapshot; such a splice would make results from different times and different materials look like outputs from the same input instance.

```text
Old record ───────┐
               ├── Current entry point ──> Current revision (first check)
Original input ───────┘        \
                         └────> Current revision (second check)

Recovery page: a path that was usable later
```

The two revision lines in the diagram represent only the two results being compared at the time, not two newly created versions or the names of two long-term states. The recovery page is placed outside the diagram to emphasize that it belongs to a different kind of record: it shows later usability and cannot be brought back into the diagram as the value from either the first or the second check.

## Narrowing the Impact

The capacity baseline, resource curves, and regression localization are adjacent areas of work within the Performance Lab. When the entry-point divergence was first discovered, the fact that they were often reviewed together was not sufficient to conclude that all three were affected in the same way. The existing materials did not support that scope assessment.

The scope used in this record is "the record returned by the current entry point cannot be treated as the same state at the two observation points." This scope is sufficient to explain why the original comparison stopped and why the old record was retained; it is not sufficient to establish that the resource curves had degraded or that the capacity baseline had changed.

An entry point returning different revision values removes the single reference point for a comparison based on the old record. Losing that single reference point does not mean that all subsequent work is impossible. The capacity baseline, resource curves, and regression localization can still be reviewed separately, but every new result must be recorded separately from the initial divergence and must not be silently added to the old incident snapshot.

The recovery page also cannot be used to expand or reduce the impact. It only records that a usable path existed later. Describing that fact as "the work area has returned to normal" would go beyond what the recovery page itself supports; conversely, describing the initial difference in values as "the entire lab was unavailable" would likewise go beyond the preserved scope.

The role of the independent schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria here is to establish that the Performance Lab can retain its own anomaly records and recovery assessments. They are neither the cause of this discrepancy nor a basis for determining how other work items should be attributed.

## Withdrawal of the Initial Assessments

The earliest verbal assessment leaned toward "the entry point is just refreshing slowly." This assessment was not retained as a conclusion. Different values returned by the current entry point at two points in time could indeed have resulted only from a state update, but the incident materials did not contain enough continuous records to prove this. Writing a possibility as an explanation would hide the part of the connection between the old record and the new entry point that still had not been established.

Another easy conclusion would be that the old record was no longer trustworthy. No materials support this either. The old record serves as evidence of the initial observation; the current entry point supplies the result seen during a later check. Their difference does not automatically invalidate either one. Instead, it shows that they cannot be interchanged without explanation.

Another inaccurate way to close the matter would be to classify the initial divergence as a transient event that had disappeared, simply because a usable path existed later. There is no confirmed connection between the usable path and the initial entry-point state. Recovery changes what can be established later; it does not change the discrepancy already preserved in the initial incident snapshot.

The published version does not turn these withdrawn assessments into a new list of candidate root causes. The existing materials are insufficient to compare the probabilities of multiple causes. The reason for preserving the withdrawal process is straightforward: later readers need to know why "refresh differences," "an error in the old record," and "recovery is enough to close the case" were not accepted as final explanations.

The draft's wording "stopped further retries" could also be misread as stopping the investigation. Its actual meaning was to stop the repeated attempts that changed the state visible in the initial incident snapshot. After saving the materials, it was still possible to retrace the entry point, organize the recovery page, or add new results; those actions simply could no longer be labeled as part of the first comparison.

## Actions Taken and Recovery Assessment

This page starts from a very narrow entry point: a new maintainer first opens the repository's public entry point at clock-ui, then follows only one direct caller. The route is currently written as follows:

```text
clock-ui repository public entry point
  |
  | Follow one direct call
  v
Direct caller
  |
  | Verify the direction in which the same object is passed
  v
The first real consumer in the team's public-entry maintenance
```

Here, "one direct call" has a precise code-reading meaning: the public entry point can identify the location of the next actual handoff, rather than merely showing an export with the same name or a type reference. `backend/src/api/mempool.ts` is still an object that should be checked on this route. The file itself provides locating material for the mempool state diff. When reading it, first identify the state currently being traced, then check what the diff does at this location: it may be received, passed to the next hop, or only constructed locally. These three cases have different implications for tracing back the entry point and must not be treated as one simply because `diff` appears in all three.

A practical review can leave a small local record:

- Which direct call does the public entry point of clock-ui point to?
- Is the object passed by the direct call still the state being traced?
- Does `backend/src/api/mempool.ts` receive this object, or another state with the same name?
- Can a receiving location be identified after the diff?
- Has that receiving location already entered the scope of the team's public-entry maintenance?

The first two determine whether the file can be put back on the route, and the last two determine whether it can be called a real consumer. This order is shorter than listing all relevant files first and also avoids treating search results as call relationships. If the diff is only generated at the current location, without receiving an object from the previous hop, leave it in a side note and do not invent a next stop along it.

Files with the same name have two uses: they can help later readers find the search terms used previously, and they can help compare the shape of the state diff.
